items.title: Intelligent Financial Forecasting Using Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Techniques
items.abstract: Financial forecasting is a core aspect of contemporary financial systems, and it helps to support some of the most important activities of a financial system, including investment planning, portfolio optimization, and risk management. The traditional forecasting models, which are mainly statistical and econometric models, are often based on assumptions of linearity and limited datasets and therefore have limited capability to accurately model the complex, volatile and nonlinear behaviour of financial markets. This paper will give a detailed comparison and contrast of the different AI and ML methods used in financial forecasting, such support vectors machines (SVM), artificial neural networks (ANN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, reinforcement learning (RL) and natural language processing (NLP). Overall, this paper demonstrates that AI and ML can have a transformative potential in the context of financial forecasting because it has the potential to develop more intelligent, responsive and efficient financial decision-making systems.

items.title: Interpretable by Design Tabular Prediction via In-Context Local Linear Learning
items.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) lets tabular foundation models make predictions without dataset-specific training or fine-tuning. These models achieve strong predictive accuracy, but interpreting how individual features contribute to the prediction remains difficult. In biology, for example, feature contributions can help identify biomarkers or risk genes. Post-hoc interpretability methods assign feature importance scores, but these scores do not indicate what the model actually uses and can lead to explanation errors. We introduce TICL$^3$ (Tabular In-Context Local Linear Learning), an interpretable-by-design predictor that uses a tabular foundation model to guide a simple linear prediction rule. TICL$^3$ first learns a shared linear model to capture dataset-level feature effects. Then, for each query, it retrieves similar training samples using representations from the foundation model and fits a second linear model to the residuals in that neighborhood. The shared model captures broad effects, while the local model corrects errors among similar samples. Their combined coefficients determine each feature contribution to the final query-specific linear score, so the same model makes and explains the prediction. Across 386 classification benchmark-dataset evaluations, TICL$^3$ trails TabICLv2 by 1.1 percentage points and outperforms CatBoost in 266 evaluations. It improves average support F1 over MAPLE by 4.7 points and achieves the best performance on both real-data selected-feature utility metrics.

items.title: Introduction
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has disrupted established assessment practices in higher education, producing widespread uncertainty about what counts as appropriate student work and how it should be evaluated. The introductory chapter argues that this uncertainty is not simply a temporary lack of clarity but reflects a deeper challenge in how assessment distinguishes between student achievement and the tools students use. Drawing on the idea of wicked problems, it suggests that this challenge cannot be definitively resolved, but must instead be worked through in context by focusing on how boundaries in assessment are being drawn, interpreted, and contested under AI conditions. This introduction uses this framing to orient the chapters that follow, showing how they contribute to understanding and respond to these changes from different perspectives. The volume that follows then brings together conceptual, empirical, and forward-looking work to examine how assessment is evolving, why these changes matter, and how educators might respond. Rather than offering a single model of AI-ready assessment, it provides a set of resources for understanding the problem and navigating it in practice.

items.title: Introduction
items.abstract: This introduction sets out the problem the book addresses: the absence of a comprehensive framework under African human rights law governing the use of artificial intelligence by social media platforms. It situates that problem within the rapid global adoption of artificial intelligence across public and private sectors, the proliferation of national and regional strategies and ethical principles, and the African vision on the regulation of artificial intelligence and emerging technologies. It explains why social media platforms occupy a central place in this debate, given business models built on retention and the suitability of artificial intelligence for inference, personalisation, and targeting at scale. The introduction then sets out the book’s structure, explaining the selection of three rights most affected by these technologies, and the rationale for treating each according to the developmental stage of the right within African jurisprudence.

items.title: Introduction to AI-Driven Multimodal Systems
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of artificial intelligence is pushing beyond unimodal paradigms, paving the way for sophisticated multimodal systems that can process and relate information from diverse sources such as text, images, audio, and sensor data. This chapter serves as a foundational introduction to AI-driven multimodal intelligence, outlining the core principles, architectures, and transformative potential of these systems. We begin by defining key concepts, contrasting multimodal learning with traditional unimodal approaches, and highlighting the inherent challenges of data heterogeneity, alignment, and fusion. The chapter then delves into the primary technical architectures for multimodal integration, including early, late, and hybrid fusion strategies, with a focus on modern neural approaches like cross-modal attention and transformers. Beyond the algorithms, we discuss the critical pipeline from data processing and feature extraction to model training and cross-modal reasoning. Finally, the chapter sets the stage for the rest of the book by underscoring the real-world implications of this technology, from enhancing accessibility to revolutionizing human–computer interaction, while also acknowledging the ongoing research challenges in robustness, interpretability, and ethical deployment.

items.title: Investigating ChatGPT’s Impact on Developing the Tertiary-Level English Department Students’ EFL Writing Skills
items.abstract: Despite the growing body of research involving examining teachers’ and students’ experiences of AI integration in EFL writing pedagogy in Bangladesh, relatively little is known about English department students’ perceptions of ChatGPT’s influence in major domains of EFL writing. To bridge this gap, our research investigates tertiary-level English department students’ perceptions of ChatGPT’s impact in developing their EFL writing skills within the Bangladeshi context through employing a mixed-method research design, comprising both quantitative and qualitative data. Quantitative data were collected from 74 undergraduate and graduate students at a public university in Bangladesh using a structured five-point Likert-scale questionnaire and subsequently, qualitative insights were gathered to supplement the survey data through three focus group discussions (FGDs). Our study explored ChatGPT’s perceived role across four key domains of EFL writing: motivation and engagement, grammatical correction, writing essays and creating references. Findings revealed that ChatGPT positively influenced students’ motivation through providing immediate and non-judgmental feedback, facilitating idea generation, content organization and context-specific writing. Also, ChatGPT facilitated the pre-writing and foundational stages of essay writing. Students exhibited more caution regarding ChatGPT’s role as a grammar correction and referencing tool. Despite its usefulness in explaining grammar rules and providing language-related feedback, students found specialized grammar correction tools to be more reliable than ChatGPT. Likewise, ChatGPT emerged as an unreliable referencing tool due to producing misleading citation information. Our study offers key implications for educators, stakeholders and policy- makers to integrate ChatGPT more ethically and effectively in EFL writing while preserving independent reasoning and judicious evaluation. items.title: Investigating the Effect of User Onboarding and Task Demonstration on Training Performance and Learning in a Multiuser AR Learning Environment
items.abstract: Collaborative augmented reality (AR) systems are increasingly used for technical training, yet limited evidence exists on how instructional design choices affect learning and transfer. This study examined the effects of onboarding strategy and task demonstration modality in a multiuser AR environment for motor control unit setup and lockout-tagout training. Eighty participants were assigned to one of four conditions in a 2 × 2 between-subjects study: checklist versus interactive onboarding and video versus avatar-based demonstration. Participants completed AR-based training and then performed the procedure on physical equipment. Results showed that avatar-based demonstrations produced significantly greater learning gains, while video-based demonstrations produced fewer procedural errors during physical transfer. Onboarding strategy did not significantly affect objective learning or transfer outcomes. These findings reveal an important design tradeoff: immersive avatar demonstrations may strengthen conceptual understanding, whereas physically grounded video demonstrations may better support real-world procedural transfer. The study provides evidence-based guidance for designing collaborative AR training systems in technical workforce education.

items.title: Investigating the Efficacy of the Gemini 2.5 Pro Model in the Estimation of Macronutrient Content
items.abstract: Health guidance is a topic that has been gaining increasing traction in the past few years. Specifically, apps utilizing AI to provide health guidance and allow users to track macronutrient content have been gaining prevalence in recent research. However, current apps require users to manually input all information into the app. Therefore, this work seeks to evaluate the effectiveness of the Gemini 2.5 Pro model, a multimodal large language model (LLM), in analyzing the macronutrient content (i.e., proteins, fats, and carbohydrates) in food images. We tested 100 dishes randomly sampled from the Nutrition5k dataset. Each image was queried three times with three different prompt phrasings and the estimated values were compared with the ground truth values in the dataset. For the baseline prompt, the mean absolute error (MAE) was 4.1 g for protein, 3.6 g for fat, and 6.1 g for carbohydrates, and the median absolute percentage errors were 29.9%, 29.2%, and 32.1% respectively. The mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) was 38.5% for protein but 211.2% for fats and 442.7% for carbohydrates, which were inflated due to a small number of dishes containing less than 0.5 g of fat or carbohydrate, where errors of a few grams produced errors in the thousands. Without dishes with less than 2 g of the nutrient, the MAPE was 38.5%, 33.6%, and 33.5%. On metrics not sensitive to near-zero values, error was of similar size across the three macronutrients, and protein was underestimated on average, with the largest errors concentrated in a subset of dishes. MAE differed by at most 0.6 g across prompt wordings, although fat MdAPE was higher under both alternative prompts. Because no confidence intervals or significance tests were computed, these are observations from a single 100-dish sample rather than established differences. Additionally, the 100 dishes selected for the study came from a 400-dish subset whose selection cannot be reproduced.

items.title: Investigating the Utility of LLM-Based “Silicon Samples” in Political Science Conjoint Experiments
items.abstract: Abstract This research note is the first study to explore the viability of using LLM-generated respondents in forced-choice conjoint experiments. I generate naive “silicon samples” using three models, GPT 4o-Mini, Llama 3.2, and Magistral-small-2506, benchmarked to a large sample of live conjoint respondents, allowing for direct comparisons between human and silicon choices. The resulting analyses suggest that naively generated silicon samples are insufficient to simulate human decision-making in conjoint tasks; these results also suggest that there are systemic differences in the way demographic covariates shape LLM and human choices in experimental contexts. In total, this analysis makes two important contributions: it establishes a descriptive baseline understanding of LLM-generated respondent performance in conjoint experiments and suggests that naive silicon samples cannot accurately infer human choices using demographic traits in experimental decision making contexts. Finally, the implications of these results imply that LLMs consider covariates differently than live respondents do in micro-level decision making contexts.

items.title: Investigation Management
items.abstract: This chapter examines the principles and structures that underpin effective investigation management, and it emphasises that organised processes, robust governance, and strategic oversight enhance investigative success and safeguard justice. It outlines governance frameworks, clarifies the role of the (P)GSB, and establishes an Overarching Investigative Strategy that integrates major incident rooms, allocates appropriate resources, and defines enquiry team roles. The chapter defines aims, objectives, and terms of reference, and it explains how investigators prioritise lines of enquiry, manage information flow, and maintain clear and consistent communication across complex operations. It describes action management systems, situation reporting, and handover procedures, and it promotes organisational learning alongside the careful use of artificial intelligence to support efficiency and decision-making. Finally, the chapter addresses disclosure obligations and demonstrates that disciplined management, transparent processes, and continuous evaluation ensure accountability, reduce error, and maintain investigative integrity.

items.title: Is Gen AI an editor or a revision tool? A case study of EFL students in AI-assisted revision
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) tools become increasingly integrated into language education, understanding how learners respond to AI-generated feedback during writing revision has become an important research concern. Existing studies have primarily examined the effects of AI on writing performance, with less attention to learners’ reported decision-making and reflection during revision. This qualitative study investigated learner-AI interaction, reported revision practices and learner perceptions among 18 first-year non-English-major students enrolled in a university EFL writing course. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews following a Gen AI-assisted revision task and analysed using thematic analysis. The findings identified three interaction patterns with Gen AI: passive AI reliance, adaptive AI engagement, metacognitive AI engagement. Participants differed in how they evaluated and used AI-generated feedback, including passive acceptance, selective uptake, and critical evaluation. Some reported increased confidence, motivation, and awareness of linguistic form, whereas others expressed concerns about overreliance, authorship, and loss of personal voice. These self-reported experiences provide insight into how EFL learners perceive and manage GenAI-assisted revision, highlighting the need for pedagogical approaches that foster critical AI literacy and reflective learner autonomy.

items.title: It Takes Two to Probe, Thousands to Retrieve: Putting Vision--Language Probes to the Retrieval Test
items.abstract: Vision--language models (VLMs) are tested for fine-grained understanding with image--text matching probes, a model must prefer the correct image or caption over handcrafted negative. In retrieval, the correct item must beat thousands of alternatives. We measure how these two evaluation methods relate by using two probing benchmarks, \svo{} and SugarCrepe, for retrieval tasks. For 100 image and caption queries we judge the top-10 retrievals from full dataset of six VLMs, with human annotators and an LLM assessor. We than compare how well models rank pool of items on the same queries, while changing only where the negatives comes from: the benchmark, a random draw, or the judged-incorrect retrievals of other models. On \svo{} the accuracy of retrieving a positive over handcrafted negatives is significantly higher than for retrieved ones (the correct item is preferred in 85\% against 77\% of the time). Using pool of ten retrieved negatives leads to same accuracy as when one uses pool of 200 to 430 random negatives. On SugarCrepe the order is reversed: its handcrafted negatives are harder than the retrieved ones. Incomplete relevance labels explain most of the low retrieval scores on \svo{}, where the top-ranked item is correct for 54--90\% of the queries under human labels against 6--21\% under the benchmark's labels. However, we detect no association between passing the probe for a query and retrieving a correct item first. The LLM assessor o3 agrees with individual annotators ($κ$ 0.57--0.61) slightly less than they agree with each other (0.64--0.68).

items.title: It’s Not the Tool, It’s the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems can now reliably solve many standard tasks used in introductory physics courses, producing correct equations, graphs, and explanations. While this capability is often framed as an opportunity for efficiency or personalization, it also poses a subtle ethical and educational risk: students may increasingly submit correct results without engaging in the epistemic practices that define learning physics. This challenge has recently been described as the "boiling frog problem" because we may not fully recognize how rapidly AI capabilities are advancing and fail to respond with commensurate urgency. In this article, we argue that the central challenge of AI in physics education is not cheating or tool selection, but instructional design. Drawing on research on self-regulated learning, cognitive load, multiple representations, and hybrid intelligence, we propose a practical framework for cognitively activated learning activities that structures student activities before, during, and after AI use. Using an example from an introductory kinematics laboratory, we show how AI can be integrated in ways that preserve prediction, interpretation, and evaluation as core learning activities. Rather than treating AI as an answer-generating tool, the framework positions AI as an epistemic partner whose contributions are deliberately bounded and reflected upon.

items.title: Judged in Company: In-Context Batching Makes LLM Verdicts Depend on Other Items
items.abstract: To save cost, practitioners often ask a language model to grade many independent items in one prompt. This assumes that verdicts are separable: that the verdict on an item does not depend on the other items in the prompt or on its position among them. Across three judgement tasks (harm in social-media comments, short-answer grading and review star ratings) and five open-weight models with 4-9B parameters, assigning the same 2,000 items to different random batches of 25 changes 11-22% of decisions on harm and grading, 6.5-13.3 points more than renaming the item keys or rewording the instruction, while AUROC against human labels differs from single-item grading only by -0.033 to +0.010; for four models with 14-32B parameters, 6-15% of decisions change, 4.2-9.1 points more. We show that flip rates decompose exactly into components of order, slot and membership, and that under a threshold model they grow with the square root of the variance that the context contributes, so that effects that are small for scores are large for decisions. Most of the latent dissimilarity between partitions comes from the order of the neighbours and the slot. The main effect of which items share the prompt, the part that voting over permutations of a batch cannot remove, accounts for 0.11-0.22 of it, and majority votes over nine permutations still leave 52-60% of the flips. Batched verdicts also differ systematically from single-item verdicts: even the majority of fifteen random batches disagrees with them on 8.4-17.8% of decisions. Editing a single generation shows that both the model's own earlier verdicts and the neighbours' texts carry the effect. On the easy task, star ratings, only 2.9-3.9% of decisions change. We recommend grading ambiguous items one per prompt, recovering most of the cost with a cached prefix, and reporting agreement with single-item grading whenever items are batched.

items.title: Knowledge Acquisition Methods and Conceptual Mastery Outcomes in Private Institutions of Learning in Uganda
items.abstract: For one to achieve meaningful learning, Knowledge acquisition is a very crucial factor that should never be undermined, however, we should also note that the learner's possession of information does not necessarily mean that he understands all the concepts or is able to apply them in unfamiliar situations. This narrative literature review examines how knowledge acquisition methods may shape conceptual mastery in private institutions of learning in Uganda. It examines and brings together the conceptual and theoretical perspectives represented in the literature cited by different authors, including constructivist learning, deep approaches to learning, critical thinking, collaborative learning, inquiry-based learning, experiential learning, formative assessment, and technology-supported instruction. The review also looks at the advantages and disadvantages of artificial intelligence and digital knowledge-management tools. The reviewed literature consistently argues that conceptual mastery occurs when learners actively connect new material with prior knowledge, explain ideas, investigate problems, receive feedback, reflect on their learning, and transfer knowledge to authentic tasks. Lectures and other educators can provide all the necessary explanations and provide foundational knowledge, but they may not support mastery when they are used as the only instructional method or when majorly paired with recall-based examinations. items.title: LaplaceReason: A Certified Benchmark and Continuous Dynamic Systems Reasoning Suite for Frontier Large Language Models
items.abstract: Abstract: Frontier Large Language Models (LLMs) such as DeepSeek-R1, OpenAI o1/o3, and Qwen-2.5-Math have achieved near-human proficiency on discrete reasoning benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, MATH). However, they systematically exhibit catastrophic hallucination, severe phase lag, and structural divergence when evaluated on continuous dynamic systems, multiscale stiff ordinary differential equations (ODEs), and high-order operational calculus. Traditional synthetic data pipelines fail to provide reliable supervision for these domains because conventional computer algebra solvers suffer from Wilkinson's catastrophic conditioning when factorizing high-order characteristic polynomials (K > 18). In this work, we present LaplaceReason, the first certified, massive reasoning benchmark designed to evaluate and train frontier LLMs on continuous multi-physics and dynamic systems. Ground truth solutions and step-by-step reasoning trajectories are certified via a deterministic, high-precision operational oracle guaranteeing machine-precision residual bounds (||R||_inf < 10^-14) across arbitrary orders without numerical root-finding. The benchmark spans seven fundamental task families:1. High-order rational dynamics (K from 2 to 60)2. Multiscale stiff ODEs (stiffness ratio S > 100x)3. Real-time randomized SVD with universal Gavish-Donoho noise rank thresholding4. 3D tomographic C-scan reconstruction5. Sub-millisecond zero-lag kinematic trajectory extrapolation6. Matrix-pencil modal extraction without Fourier spectral leakage7. items.title: Large language models as enablers of industrial information integration in construction: an adoption mechanism study
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are emerging enablers of industrial information integration, yet their adoption mechanisms in construction remain unclear. This study develops an integrated framework that combines the Technology Acceptance Model and the Information Systems Success model, extended with trust, prior LLM experience, perceived substitution crisis, and job specialization, to explain individual adoption of LLMs for information integration in construction. Data from a cross-sectional survey of 82 Chinese construction professionals are analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling and bootstrapping. Results show that perceived ease of use robustly strengthens attitude and provides directional evidence for strengthening perceived usefulness, while perceived usefulness strengthens attitude and attitude drives intention to use. Trust, reinforced by perceived information quality, shows a positive association with intention under the primary one-tailed criterion, but this relationship requires further validation under the two-tailed robustness check. System quality and information quality indirectly foster adoption by improving perceived ease of use, although the relationship between system quality and trust is supported only as directional evidence, while prior LLM experience enhances ease of use but not perceived usefulness or trust. Perceived substitution crisis and job specialization exhibit no significant effects. The findings highlight that successful LLM-enabled information integration depends on both technical quality and psychological appraisals, and they offer implications for designing trustworthy, humancentered LLM applications that advance intelligent, interconnected construction ecosystems. The study links micro-level user acceptance with macro-level digital transformation and integration strategic objectives.

items.title: Leading Equity-Focused School and District Improvement With GenAI: The Human-AI Team Improvement Framework
items.abstract: This theoretical paper examines how educational leaders can leverage generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for equity-focused school and district improvement. Although prior improvement leadership research connects equity-focused leadership, improvement science, and workplace culture (Shepard, 2026), AI use in education remains largely focused on individual use, leaving less understood about what changes when GenAI becomes part of an improvement team. Drawing on equity-focused leadership, improvement science, workplace culture, and human-AI teaming, the paper introduces the Human-AI Team Improvement Framework. The framework centers equity-focused collaborative continuous improvement and identifies three interdependent leadership conditions (co-inquiry, empowered ownership, and courageous safety) that support humans and GenAI in working, learning, and improving together. The framework focuses attention on the leadership conditions needed for human-AI teams to work and learn together in improvement. It suggests that GenAI may help teams address immediate problems while also building their capacity to inquire, learn, and improve. The paper concludes with implications for educational leaders and directions for research on human-AI improvement teams in practice.

items.title: Leading motivational factors influencing immigrant individuals to become entrepreneurs in Sweden
items.abstract: The purpose of this study is to explore the factors motivating immigrants to migrate to Sweden and the factors influencing immigrants to become entrepreneurs in Sweden. To address this, the study include two inter-related research questions; (1) what factors influence the immigrants to migrate to Sweden? And (2) what are the leading motivational factors that influence immigrants to become entrepreneurs in Sweden? This study grounded in the push and pull theory. The push and pull theory was used to understand both the research questions, which are motivations behind immigrants’ decision to migrate to Sweden and the motivations of immigrants to become entrepreneurs in Sweden. The study has followed purely the qualitative research method in accordance with abductive approach which allowed the author to move back and forth between data and theory. Data were collected through 11 semi-structured interviews of immigrants who became entrepreneurs in Sweden. Thematic analysis was conducted to identify common patterns in the data. The findings indicate that the immigrants are motivated to migrate to Sweden as a result of expecting future prospects, educational aspirations, environment and career related opportunities and family related concerns. Further the immigrants pursue their entrepreneurial journey as a result of motivational factors such as previous influences and experiences, intrinsic motivations and personal characteristics, support system influences, financial incentives, barriers in the labour market, perceived ease of entrepreneurship and business environment related factors.

items.title: Leading the Redesign: Purpose, Ecosystems and Sequencing in School Leadership for AI
items.abstract: Most school responses to generative AI begin with tools: which platform to license, which training day to run, which policy to publish. This article argues that the order is backwards. Drawing on a practitioner newsletter series written for school leaders in 2026, read alongside research on curriculum reform and institutional change, it examines AI in schools as a leadership problem. It sets out five pressures that leaders face: a speed gap between students' adoption of AI and institutions' capacity to govern it; a purpose question about what school is for when knowledge is freely available; an ecosystem problem, in which reforms fail not at the design stage but in the system of assessment, professional learning and routines they land in; a sequencing problem, in which institutions buy tools before doing the human work that makes them useful; and a structural shift in which families increasingly unbundle schooling. It proposes a five-step leadership sequence (purpose, conversation, red lines, ecosystem align‐ ment and iteration) and argues that leaders should separate two decisions that are usually treated as one: what AI should free time for, and how fast the institution should move.

items.title: Learn First, Then Use AI: Testing an Expert Consensus on Generative AI and Learning Against the Empirical Evidence
items.abstract: Debate about generative AI in education often asks whether it is good or bad for learning. A 2026 expert consensus report from the University of Minnesota, UNC-Chapel Hill and UC Irvine argues that this question is too blunt. Thirty experts used a preregistered Delphi method to rate 65 learning processes for how likely general-purpose generative AI is to enhance or disrupt them, reaching consensus on 42. The pattern they describe can be read as a sequence: AI threatens the early work of taking in new information, can support the consolidation of what has been learned, and does not yet reliably support higher-order thinking and transfer. The report also rates the strength of the existing evidence as low. This review asks whether the experimental and observational studies published so far are consistent with that consensus. It maps a field experiment with high-school mathematics students, a randomised con‐ trolled trial of an AI physics tutor, an EEG study of essay writing, and survey research on cognitive offloading onto the three stages of the sequence. The studies largely agree with the experts. Unrestricted answer-giving harms acquisition. Tutor-style designs built on learning science can strengthen consolidation. Offloading thinking is linked with weaker critical thinking. We summarise this as a 'learn first, then use AI' principle, link it to established learning science, and set out implications for teachers, school leaders and researchers.

items.title: Learning designers and assessment practice in the age of AI
items.abstract: This chapter examines how learning designers (LDs) mediate and lead assessment transformation in higher education in response to the rise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). Drawing on cross-institutional interviews with 11 LDs from six Australian and New Zealand universities, it identifies ways that LDs are enacting their roles in response to GenAI: agents of change; emotional and cultural navigators; strategic influencers and policy shapers; designers of assessment; technical specialists and tool curators; and advocates for equity and inclusion. Situated within Whitchurch’s notion of the third space , LDs act as boundary spanners who translate institutional imperatives and academic values into coherent pedagogical practice. Their work supports transforming institutional ‘AI shock’ into opportunities for innovation, embedding authentic, reflective, and inclusive assessment practices. The chapter argues that LDs’ relational and strategic expertise is valuable in reimagining assessment for an AI-mediated educational future and calls for their recognition as co-leaders in shaping policy, pedagogy, and institutional culture.

items.title: Learning Processes in Science Teams: How Do Human-AI Scientists Learn From Each Other While Developing Collaborative AI
items.abstract: This study examines how scientists in interdisciplinary programs learn from one another during collaboration. Researchers who participated in large scale research projects on human-AI teaming were surveyed about their collaborative experiences. Survey results show that regular cross-team meetings, careful listening, and adaptive communication are central to effective integration, while terminology conflicts and coordination costs persist. Findings highlight interaction structures and integrative roles as key levers for improving interdisciplinary teamwork. Framed within the context of the science of team science, the discussion highlights the support needed for interdisciplinary structures and processes enabling effective scientific collaboration.

items.title: Learning Safe Flow Matching Robot Policies from Binary Feasibility Oracles
items.abstract: Robot foundation models increasingly rely on flow-based action generation for general-purpose manipulation, yet the generated actions are not guaranteed to satisfy physical constraints such as joint limits and collision avoidance. This problem is especially challenging when the feasible set cannot be described analytically and is accessible only through black-box feasibility oracles. We study this practical oracle-only setting and propose an oracle-guided differentiable safeguard for safe flow-matching robot policies. The safeguard uses binary feasibility queries to correct unsafe updates in the forward pass, while extracting local boundary information to provide constraint-aware learning signals in the backward pass. Combined with discrete-time flow matching, the same safeguard is used during training and inference, enabling forward--backward aligned policy learning without explicit or differentiable constraint models. Experiments on obstacle-aware robotic manipulation demonstrate 100% constraint satisfaction while preserving task performance.

items.title: Legal Safeguards for Ai-Assisted Judicial Decision-Making: A Comparative Framework of Transparency, Human Oversight and Effective Remedies
items.abstract: Abstract Courts are adopting artificial intelligence faster than lawmakers are writing rules for it. Risk scores inform bail and sentencing, language models draft summaries and sometimes reasoning, and judicial councils issue guidance in the absence of statutes. This article asks what a litigant is legally entitled to when an AI system touches the decision that affects them. Using a doctrinal and functional comparative method, we examine binding and soft-law instruments from the European Union, the Council of Europe, the United Kingdom, the United States, Brazil, Colombia and India, checked against official or reliable sources as of 26 October 2026. Three findings emerge. First, transparency duties are mostly addressed to institutions and regulators; the person whose liberty or rights are at stake rarely gets a right to know that AI was used, still less how. Second, human oversight is declared everywhere but engineered almost nowhere, despite strong evidence that nominal review produces automation bias rather than control. Third, remedies are the weakest link: with few exceptions, no instrument attaches a legal consequence to undisclosed or uncritical reliance on AI. We propose a Disclosure–Oversight–Remedy (DOR) framework that scales safeguards to the way AI is used, from auxiliary support to evaluative input, and prohibits determinative use. The framework converts principles into enforceable procedural entitlements and offers a template for legislators, judicial councils and courts.

items.title: Letting AI Formulate the Research Question: Autonomous Research Agents
items.abstract: Systems such as The AI Scientist have shown that AI agents can carry out and write up research, but in those demonstrations humans chose the research area and selected the outputs to show. We study letting the AI formulate the research question itself, and we report every run. Our system gives an off-the-shelf coding agent an instruction document and two skills: one for formulating the question, in which the agent diverges from recent technologies into problems of other fields, screens its candidates for known failure modes and obtains a critique from a different model; and one for peer review, in which a reviewer from another model family reruns the study from its records before the agent revises the paper. Over 13 development runs, changes to the one or two sentences that set the research area coincided with large shifts in what the candidate questions and the chosen papers were about, which led us to the area of a new technology applied to a societal problem. We froze the system after a pilot run and report five consecutive runs: the pilot, counted by a disclosed amendment to the pre-registration, and four pre-registered runs. All five runs went from question formulation to a revised, re-computable paper, with local computation on a laptop and no research input from humans, and external AI reviewers reading only the papers judged them at or near workshop level. We release the system, the five papers and the records needed to reproduce them.

items.title: Leveraging artificial intelligence for autonomous space healthcare: current evidence, operational architecture and research priorities for deep-space exploration
items.abstract: Introduction Deep-space missions will progressively limit real-time ground support, rapid evacuation and resupply, creating a need for medical capabilities that can operate with graded autonomy. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support this transition, but terrestrial performance cannot be equated with spaceflight readiness. Methods We conducted a narrative, hypothesis-generating review of literature relevant to AI-enabled space healthcare. Sources were selected iteratively for their contribution to health monitoring, biofluid analysis, medical imaging, clinical decision support or radiation assessment. The review did not use a systematic screening protocol or formal meta-analytic quality assessment; therefore, findings are synthesised qualitatively and claims are calibrated to evidence maturity. Results Evidence was grouped as spaceflight operational use, space-relevant prototype or analogue demonstration, terrestrial clinical validation, terrestrial experimental demonstration, or conceptual transfer. AI may support personalised monitoring, biofluid interpretation, ultrasound acquisition and analysis, radiation forecasting and clinical decision support. However, most cited applications remain terrestrial demonstrations. Key barriers include limited astronaut data, shifted physiological baselines, restricted computation and power, sensor and storage constraints, model drift, explainability, uncertainty management and failure handling. Conclusion AI is most plausibly deployed as one component of an integrated autonomous medical system that combines wearables and biosensors, onboard records, imaging, radiation monitoring, clinical decision support, crew oversight and delayed telemedical consultation. Near-term priorities are prospective validation in mission-relevant analogues, personalised baselines, resource-aware edge deployment, explicit uncertainty thresholds, human override and pre-defined safe fallback procedures. AI should augment rather than replace telemedicine and professional judgement.

items.title: Leveraging generative AI for human understanding: meta-requirements and design principles for Explanatory AI as an emerging paradigm
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly support decision-making across critical domains, yet explainable AI (XAI) approaches prioritise algorithmic transparency over human comprehension. While XAI reveals computational processes for model validation, end users require explanations integrating domain knowledge, contextual reasoning, and professional frameworks. This disconnect reveals a design challenge: existing approaches fail to address how practitioners need to understand and act upon AI recommendations. This paper introduces Explanatory AI as an emerging complementary paradigm where AI systems leverage generative and multimodal capabilities to serve as explanatory partners for human understanding. Unlike traditional XAI, which answers ‘How did the algorithm decide?’ for validation purposes, Explanatory AI addresses ‘Why does this make sense?’ for practitioners making informed decisions. Through theory-informed design, we synthesise multidisciplinary perspectives from cognitive science, communication research, and education with empirical evidence from healthcare and AI expert interviews. Our analysis identifies five dimensions distinguishing Explanatory AI from XAI: explanatory purpose, communication mode, epistemic stance, adaptivity, and cognitive design. We derive five meta-requirements and formulate ten design principles prescribing how to build such systems, illustrated through five UI mockups exemplifying implementation. Explanatory AI operates standalone or combined with XAI, serving distinct purposes in creating systems that genuinely support human reasoning and decision-making.

items.abstract: Few-Shot Action Recognition (FSAR) widely use in Action Recognition domains with limited labeled data, such as medical surgery. Existing FSAR methods often rely on single-modal approaches, which suffer from limited feature representation and a lack of semantic understanding. To overcome these limitations, we propose MoMA, a novel Mamba-based multimodal FSAR framework, designed to optimize the learning of multimodal information and improve the performance of few-shot action recognition tasks. MoMA integrates a multimodal large language model (MLLM) to generate semantically rich representations from both textual and video data, which are then aligned and fused with visual features. To address the challenges of domain-specific prior knowledge and intra-class variance, we introduce a dual-branch contrastive learning architecture that reinforces category distinctions and mitigates the accumulation of intra-class heterogeneity. Our experimental results show that MoMA outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the HMDB51, Kinetics, and SSv2 datasets, achieving improvements of 1.5%, 1.9%, and 3.5%, respectively, in the 1-shot setting.

items.title: LiveFit:
items.abstract: The rising pressure on lifestyle related illnesses including obesity, diabetes and heart diseases, has heightened pressure on the need to develop digital health solutions in an intelligent and scalable manner. The paper describes LiveFit, which is AI-enhanced customized nutrition and subscription-based health management software, which combines real-time monitoring of macronutrients, automatically adjusted diet, online ordering of meal plans, and an interface available across platforms. The suggested system adheres to a layered structure, which comprises a web-based dashboard, a Node.js-based microservice configuration and the MongoDB Atlas cloud storage, as well as a React Native (Expo Router) application. JWT-based authentication is used to ensure secure communication and brings scaling to data processing and user interactions which are facilitated by cloud-hosted APIs. The system will integrate the logic of contextual recommendation which dynamically examines nutritional intake and gives personal feedback in terms of perceived deficiencies. In contrast to other traditional calorie counting programs, LiveFit is aimed at active nutritional evaluation and dynamic intervention as opposed to passive dieting over a record. Experimental analysis proves the stable system operation, average API response time does not exceed 200 ms, and the accuracy of authentication is stable with as much as multi-user dependence. The suggested framework identifies the possibility to use artificial intelligence, cloud infrastructure, and subscription-based models to provide adaptive and scalable preventive healthcare systems.

items.title: LLM Agent-Based Design of RISC-V CPUs with FPGA-in-the-Loop Evaluation
items.abstract: Long-run RTL simulation of CPU candidates can take hours, while short diagnostic runs may miss performance degradation that emerges later in execution. This evaluation cost can delay design decisions in LLM-agent-based CPU development. We present a development environment in which LLM agents implement CPU candidates on an FPGA and use on-board performance measurements to guide design decisions. We applied it to the human-supervised development of a single-cycle RV32I core into a three-wide out-of-order RV32IM core. The final design reaches 5.61 CoreMark/MHz at 130 MHz on a Artix-7 FPGA. For the same CPU candidate running 8,000 CoreMark iterations, FPGA evaluation, including implementation, was 9.6x faster than single-threaded RTL simulation. In one case, board measurements revealed long-run performance degradation in a candidate that improved in a short diagnostic run. The result guided candidate selection and led to RTL-based root-cause analysis and a fix.

items.title: LLM eBay: A Simple and Truthful Marketplace for Fine-Tuned LLMs Trading
items.abstract: Personalized fine-tuning of Large Language Models (LLMs) enhances user experience but incurs substantial computational costs. Recent studies show that initializing training from a style-similar fine-tuned model reduces adaptation overhead, turning such checkpoints into reusable, tradable assets. A marketplace for these checkpoints, however, faces information asymmetry: sellers may misreport a checkpoint's style, while buyers cannot verify its usefulness before purchase, which invites adverse selection. We introduce LLM eBay, a simple single-round marketplace for trading fine-tuned LLMs. Sellers are paid per purchase at a posted price, and a truncated quadratic proper scoring rule adjusts each payment according to how well the seller's style report agrees with a style signal that the platform measures by generating text on hidden prompts. We show that the score elicits the verifier's expected signal, characterize exactly when truthful reporting is a seller best response under per-purchase demand, and bound the downside risk from noisy verification. In an end-to-end study with real LoRA checkpoints on two base models and three buyer tasks, LLM eBay reduces measured convergence steps by 8.5\% relative to retrieval over self-reported style (95\% CI [1.0\%, 15.9\%]). In model-based market simulations built on a measured style-to-cost relationship, it cuts style-claim error by 96.5\% (from 0.424 to 0.015), recovers 96.3\% of Oracle welfare, saves 72.4\% of the cost of fine-tuning from the base model, and keeps all providers profitable in the default setting.

items.title: LLM-guided Planar Loco-Manipulation for Quadruped Robots
items.abstract: Robotic navigation typically assumes a collision-free route to the goal exists; in cluttered environments with movable obstacles, however, reaching the goal may require physical interaction. Classical solutions encode these behaviors through geometric rules and task-specific logic, while learning-based approaches often constrain the decision space to low-dimensional motion commands or predefined action sets. We instead consider a broader decision space, jointly selecting the skill, relevant object, and geometric target. Our language-conditioned task planner, fine-tuned with LoRA on synthetic data, maps natural-language tasks and a structured scene representation to variable-length sequences of parameterized actions, executed by low-level reinforcement-learning policies. The planner learns the geometric relations underlying interactive navigation and outperforms a classical planner and a prompted frontier model on interactive navigation tasks. Comparisons with models trained from scratch indicate that composition does not require pretraining when the representation is structured, whereas pretraining yields more reliable geometric targets. At the low level, we introduce an end-to-end whole-body planar pushing policy that achieves a 93.3% success rate in simulation, versus 83.5% for a hierarchical baseline, while reducing completion time by more than 60%. On hardware, the hierarchy yields the correct skill composition in 44/45 trials and end-to-end success in 34/45. items.title: Looking ahead: new approaches to the diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation of patients with deep infiltrating endometriosis
items.abstract: Deep infiltrating endometriosis (DIE) is a severe form of endometriosis characterized by deep infiltration of endometriotic tissue into the retroperitoneal space and muscular walls of pelvic organs. Its nonspecific clinical presentation and the limited sensitivity of standard diagnostic methods contribute to significant diagnostic delays, while current treatments are primarily symptomatic and associated with high recurrence rates. This review summarizes current and emerging approaches to the diagnosis of DIE, including molecular markers, high-resolution imaging techniques, standardized protocols and classifications, and artificial intelligence-based algorithms. Potential therapeutic targets involved in the pathogenesis of DIE are discussed, including the PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling pathway, microRNAs, fibrogenic factors, and specific immune mechanisms. items.title: Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence Models for Fracture Detection in the Lower Limb on Plain Radiographs - An Umbrella Review of Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) systems -predominantly deep convolutional neural networks (CNN), and more recently vision transformers (ViT) and vision–language models have been applied extensively to fracture detection on plain radiographs. As primary studies have proliferated, numerous systematic reviews and meta-analyses have appeared, each pooling overlapping sets of primary studies and reaching conclusions that are not always concordant. The lower limb comprising the hip and proximal femur, femoral shaft and distal femur, knee and patella, tibia and fibula, ankle, and foot is clinically important and heterogeneous: some regions such as the hip and ankle are comparatively well studied, whereas others such as the foot, patella, and isolated fibula fractures are under-represented in the review-level literature. An umbrella review - a systematic synthesis of existing systematic reviews rather than of primary studies is the appropriate design to map this fragmented evidence base, characterise its consistency, quantify overlap between reviews, and appraise the methodological quality of the reviews themselves. This protocol specifies, in advance, the objectives, eligibility criteria, search strategy, appraisal instruments, data-extraction framework, overlap assessment, and synthesis plan, in order to minimise post-hoc decision-making and to support transparent, reproducible conduct. Status at registration: searches are complete (August to October 2026); title and abstract screening is in progress, having commenced on 16 October 2026; full-text screening and data extraction have not begun. This registration is therefore submitted for research that is underway, with the current state disclosed.

items.title: Machine Learning and Explainable AI for Slope Stability Assessment: A Systematic Review of Methods, Parameters, and Research Gaps
items.abstract: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly used to predict the factor of safety (FoS) and stability state of slopes, often combined with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). This PRISMA 2020 systematic review searched OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and Crossref (2000–2026), screened 6,550 unique records, mapped 1,009 eligible studies at abstract level and synthesised 137 open-access full texts. Publications grew sharply after 2020, and artificial neural networks are giving way to tree ensembles, deep learning and metaheuristic hybrids. Reported performance is high (median test 2 0.97; median accuracy 0.93) but rests mainly on synthetic limit-equilibrium or finite-element data (51 % of studies) or on small, overlapping compilations of published case histories (median 190 cases). Only 11 % of studies addressed data quality or duplicates, 39 % used cross-validation, 4 % validated on independent cases and 15 % shared code or data. Class thresholds ranged from FoS 1.0 to 1.3. About half of the studies reported explanations, mostly feature importance, sensitivity analysis or SHAP, but none validated them quantitatively against limit-equilibrium sensitivities. Priorities are curated public datasets, leakage-aware and external validation, explicit target definitions, uncertainty quantification and mechanics-based validation of explanations. items.title: Managing AI-Driven Brand Transformation: Developing an Integrated Change Management Model for Organizational Brand Renewal in India
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing experience design, process coordination, and strategic identity communication in organizations. Whereas there has been a trend in brand-related research focusing on the impact of AI-based personalization, automation, and customer interaction, change management research has mainly concentrated on digital transformation, adaptability, and capability development. However, little research connects the topic of organizational changes in AI with brand renewal. Thus, this paper bridges this gap through developing and demonstrating an integrated framework for managing AI-based brand transformation in Indian organizations. Building on ADKAR model, dynamic capabilities theory, agile change management, digital transformation maturity, internal branding, employee brand ambassadorship, and the AI-revised Brand Identity Prism developed by Kapferer, this paper puts forward the AI-Brand Change Framework (ABCF). In addition to the theoretical progress, in the manuscript an agent-based simulation is provided in which 168 diverse organizational agents are developed based on the framework’s causal logic. The simulation is a test of theoretical consistency, not an empirical test. Internally consistent and implementable, the framework suggests that digital sophistication, adaptive capabilities, nimble change management, ADKAR congruence, internal brand stewardship, employee brand advocacy, and AI-driven brand recognition correlate positively with brand rejuvenation in the simulated agent cohort. The study contributes to the knowledge by linking the concepts of branding and change management, applying the theory of internal branding within the framework of AI-driven situations and proposing an operational model for organizations undergoing AI-driven transformation. The research also includes a step-by-step guide to implementation, a diagnostic tool with indicative KPIs and policy recommendations for Indian businesses.

items.title: Mapping AI related research in education through bibliometric analysis across four selected journals from 2020 to 2025
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence in education (AIED) has expanded rapidly since the emergence of generative artificial intelligence, yet recent development remains insufficiently mapped. This study examines publication growth, thematic change, citation impact, journal profiles and collaboration structure in AI-related research published in four selected journals between 2020 and 2025: Interactive learning environments (ILE), Computers and education: artificial intelligence (CAEAI), Journal of learning analytics (JLA) and International journal of artificial intelligence in education (IJAIED). Because three venues also publish broader educational technology research, 2719 Scopus records were screened using an explicit AI-relevance criterion; 1397 publications were retained and 1322 excluded. AI-relevant output rose from 54 publications in 2020 to 558 in 2025, a 10.3-fold increase and 59.5% compound annual growth rate. Eight predefined lexical themes matched 60.3% of the corpus and therefore provide lower-bound counts; generative AI and large language models grew from 1 publication in 2020–2021 to 307 in 2024–2025 and recorded the largest count among the eight themes. Keyword clustering placed generative AI in the motor-theme quadrant. Co-authorship analysis identified a fragmented prolific core of 74 authors in the largest connected component, divided into eight sub-groups and linked by authors with high betweenness centrality. The findings characterize AI-related literature in these four journals rather than the AIED field as a whole, and the observed growth is temporally associated with, but not shown to be caused by, the release of ChatGPT.

items.title: Mapping the Integration, Impacts, and Determinants of Artificial Intelligence in Science Education: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Background: AI is increasingly examined as a tool for science-specific instruction, feedback, inquiry and teacher preparation, but research designs and claimed outcomes vary. Methods: This systematic literature review applied PRISMA 2020 reporting to a title-only Scopus search through Watase Uake on 5 September 2026. Two phrases retrieved 123 and 114 raw records, respectively (237 total). Searches were restricted to Q1 journal publications dated 2023–2026. The initial selection retained 49 articles; eight were removed in a subsequent science-education relevance audit. Two further Q1-indexed Scopus reports identified outside the Watase export were assessed but excluded as unrelated plant-science research. The final corpus comprised 41 articles, synthesized descriptively and thematically with study designs differentiated. Results: The literature describes AI as a scaffold for inquiry, dialogic science reasoning, multimodal representation, feedback, learning analytics and science-teacher preparation. Some primary studies report context-dependent benefits for measured learning outcomes, but findings cannot be generalized across heterogeneous designs. Conclusions: Appropriate science-specific pedagogy, human–AI interaction, teacher competence and ethical oversight are central considerations.

items.title: MAServeBench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Serving Systems with Hierarchical Collaboration Workloads
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) coordinate specialized agents to solve complex tasks, turning each user request into interdependent model and tool operations. Unlike independent requests, these operations become ready at different times and consume evolving context as agents coordinate and exchange results. This creates changing patterns of concurrency, computation, and memory demand that can expose different bottlenecks in LLM serving hardware. Yet benchmarking these effects requires capturing the collaboration rules that generate serving workloads, beyond the requests observed during execution. We present MAServeBench, a benchmark that treats multi-agent collaboration as a configurable dimension of serving workloads for LLM serving and hardware evaluation. Its composable stages capture how agents coordinate and exchange context in documented MAS workflows, enabling native executions to generate different workloads even when task inputs and tools remain unchanged. Hierarchical Semantic Traces preserve realized operations and dependencies for reproducible comparisons of legal release constraints at fixed work. Task-linked measurements connect these workloads to serving execution and GPU/NPU hardware behavior, revealing why serving efficiency does not always translate into timely task completion. The benchmark code is available at https://github.com/ShengxuanQiu/MAServeBench.

items.title: Measurement validity induction: a issues in the assessment, and measuring constructs through scales and instruments
items.abstract: The importance of the psychometric properties of measures in applied and basic research in the social sciences, particularly in psychology, seems to have increased with the widespread access to these procedures and their growing dissemination worldwide. Nonetheless, the availability and use of these measures may be problematic for researchers. In this paper, we propose the concept of measurement validity induction as a conceptual tool to describe the omission or inappropriate application of measurement validity results obtained in one context to justify the use and interpretation of the same measures in different contexts. In general, this involves the risk of using irrelevant information to justify the use or interpretation of a measure, that is, advocating for validity when it may not exist. Several examples from the published literature on scale validations are analyzed to detect measurement validity induction in the areas of clinical practice, occupational health, and user satisfaction. With this definition (measurement validity induction), we argue for the need to report minimum parameters of the validity of a measure in a new context beyond those reported in manuals or previous studies.

items.title: Measuring what matters in AI-integrated higher education
items.abstract: It has all but become a cliché now to say that the proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) presents significant challenges to assessment practices in higher education. While concerns about academic integrity have dominated the discourse to date, these new technologies have introduced a broader range of assessment issues that require addressing. In this chapter, we argue that the focus should transition from detecting academic dishonesty to reconsidering what student learning is and how it might be inferred through assessment. Validity and security remain essential components of accountable and trustworthy assessment regimes in a time of AI. However, the emergence of GenAI and AI agents necessitates renewed attention to learning processes in addition to outcomes. Assumptions about what can and should be measured, and what criteria are appropriate, must evolve as learning processes transform in response to AI integration. This chapter argues for the need to address questions of measurement validity before considering how assessment can be implemented to make more accurate inferences about learning in environments where AI tools function as collaborative partners in the educational experience rather than merely as potential avenues for academic misconduct.

items.abstract: Abstract Protein oxidation (PO) is a major biochemical process in meat, affecting color, texture, water-holding capacity, digestibility, flavor, and safety. This review integrates the molecular mechanisms of meat protein oxidation, including free-radical chain reactions, metal-catalyzed Fenton chemistry, lipid–protein crosstalk, and enzymatic pathways. It discusses how direct ROS/RNS attack and secondary aldehyde adduction cause structural and functional damage, with dose-, matrix-, pH-, and temperature-dependent effects that can be beneficial at mild levels but detrimental when excessive. Health implications of dietary oxidized proteins are critically evaluated, distinguishing biomarker associations, animal-model mechanisms, and limited human causal evidence. Natural antioxidants, encapsulation, nonthermal processing, and combined strategies are assessed for controlling oxidation. Advanced analytical and artificial intelligence -based approaches are also highlighted. Finally, key knowledge gaps and future directions are outlined to support precise quality and safety management in muscle foods.

items.title: Meta-learning-based reinforcement learning with deterministic voltage clamping for global MPPT in grid-connected solar PV systems
items.abstract: Rapid solar photovoltaic (PV) grid integration requires robust global maximum power point tracking (GMPPT) under partial shading conditions (PSCs). Traditional continuous reinforcement learning (RL) controllers rely on static hyperparameters, rendering them susceptible to local peak trapping and power oscillations during rapid environmental transients. To resolve these computational and dynamic limitations, this paper presents a meta-learning-based reinforcement learning framework featuring an adaptive meta-deep deterministic policy gradient (AM-DDPG) controller for simultaneous GMPPT and automated voltage regulation in grid-connected PV systems. The core algorithmic novelty is an outer meta-learning layer governed by meta-plasticity principles that dynamically tunes the inner DDPG agent’s hyperparameters through a power–duty-cycle sensitivity gradient. To bridge advanced artificial intelligence with physical hardware safety standards, a deterministic override layer strictly clamps intermediate DC-link voltage fluctuations within safe operating limits (500 V–600 V). A grid-forming (GFM) inverter stage completes the system, providing autonomous synchronization through decentralized droop mechanisms. Evaluated under complex, time-varying, real-world shading profiles, the AM-DDPG framework consistently achieves 99.4%-99.8% tracking efficiency, converges within 12 ms, and suppresses the steady-state DC-link voltage ripple by 62% compared with conventional DDPG. These findings highlight a safe, computationally efficient AI control solution for resilient energy extraction in modern power grids.

items.title: Migrants’ Religious Rights in the Algorithmic City: A European Legal Perspective
items.abstract: European cities increasingly use digital platforms, predictive analytics and artificial intelligence to allocate welfare, regulate mobility, plan public space and support security. This article examines how these systems reshape migrants’ effective enjoyment of freedom of religion or belief. Using doctrinal and comparative legal analysis, informed by interdisciplinary scholarship, it connects European human-rights law, EU data-protection and equality law, the Artificial Intelligence Act, and scholarship on urban religious diversity. The analysis identifies three recurring risks: the digital invisibility of minority religious needs in planning and service design; proxy and intersectional discrimination in welfare, housing, education and integration systems; and chilling effects produced by biometric and data-intensive surveillance of religious dress, assembly and worship. Documented institutional practices and adjudicated cases are expressly distinguished from hypothetical legal stress tests used to identify foreseeable pathways of rights interference. The article also shows that urban technology can improve access, coordination and participation when governed through transparent, accessible and contestable procedures. It proposes a rights-based model centred on infrastructural neutrality, religion-sensitive impact assessment, participatory co-design, data minimisation, meaningful explanation, accountable human review and effective remedies. It argues that religious freedom in the algorithmic city depends not only on the legality of individual decisions, but also on the design and governance of the digital infrastructures through which urban membership is recognised and administered. The European focus is methodologically deliberate: the Council of Europe and EU systems supply distinct yet interacting standards for digitally mediated municipal action. The article specifies when a technological disadvantage engages Article 9 ECHR rather than principally privacy, equality or administrative law, differentiates risks by migration status, and tests the proposed principle against two legally bounded institutional examples.

items.title: Mind The Gap (MTG-AD): Dataset and Fine-grained Evaluation for End-to-End Inline Audio Descriptions
items.abstract: Audio descriptions (AD) are essential for making visual media accessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) users. While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer a scalable solution for generating audio descriptions on-demand, their performance on ``inline'' audio descriptions -- which must fit within existing silences in a video -- remains under-explored, particularly for diverse user-generated content (UGC). We present a comprehensive investigation into MLLM-generated inline audio descriptions. First, we introduce MTG-AD, a professionally annotated dataset of 36 hours of videos, each averaging $\sim$5 mins. and 8k+ descriptions in total, co-created by paired blind and sighted AD professionals to provide a high-quality benchmark for this task. Second, we propose MTG-AD-Eval, an evaluation framework based on audio description expert guidelines that provides fine-grained, reference-free actionable metrics for model improvement. Crucially, our framework evaluates the end-to-end task: it renders the generated scripts into audio tracks to assess their fit within the original video's natural silences, minimizing disruptive overlaps. Our analysis across frontier MLLMs reveals that while models accurately describe visual events and substantially reduce speech overlaps, gaps persist in narrative pacing and flow. Finally, we empirically validate that our automated and reference-free metrics correlate significantly with human quality ratings from sighted raters and 7 BLV participants, finding that while users narrowly prefer human-authored audio descriptions, they find MLLM-generated audio descriptions highly beneficial for comprehension. We provide actionable system design guidance and release MTG-AD at https://hf.co/datasets/google/mind-the-gap-inline-ad and MTG-AD-Eval at https://github.com/google/mtg-ad.

items.title: Mobilizing the Archive: Bitext Extraction at Scale from Archival Documents for Extremely Low-resource Languages
items.abstract: While mining parallel sentences from web pages has proven effective for low-resource machine translation, the majority of the world's languages have little to no web presence. What they do have, though, are resources that are the result of centuries of efforts by linguists, such as grammars, dictionaries, and other documentation materials. We propose extracting translation examples from such linguistic resources, which offer parallel data for languages under-represented online and could potentially scale to thousands more languages. We develop a pipeline to achieve this, leveraging an Optical Character Recognition (OCR) model as well as a vision language model (VLM), to ensure identified content to be aligned with visual layout information. We demonstrate the utility of the extracted bitexts for bootstrapping translation systems across 20 languages, both by training machine translation models and by applying in-context learning for large language models. For in-context learning, we observe improvements of +15.78 and +6.94 chrF2++ over zero-shot translation for into low- and high-resource languages, respectively.

items.title: MoBiTDE: A Molecular Bilinear Two-Tower Network for Drug-Excipient Nanoparticle Co-Assembly Prediction
items.abstract: Up to 40% of clinical candidates are poorly-soluble drugs, which rely heavily on nanoparticle formulations for oral and targeted delivery. Successful formulation largely depends on the co-assembly of drug and excipients into stable nanostructures. However, traditional wet-lab trial-and-error approaches require months, even years for discoveries to be made, with a substantial cost in raw materials. From research, there are 1440 high-throughput screening pairs of drug combination, but few AI algorithms have been applied to this task, especially with the rapidly evolving chemistry large language model (LLM), which hasn’t been evaluated on this task yet. Herein, I introduce the novel application of chemistry foundation model representations to drug-excipient nanoparticle co-assembly prediction. Specifically, this essay introduces MoBiTDE, a molecular bilinear two-tower network designed to learn pairwise compatibility between drugs and excipients. MoBiTDE employs frozen SMI-TED embeddings as pre-trained molecular representations, complemented by 24 RDKit-derived physicochemical descriptors. Drugs and excipient representations are processed through two independent molecular towers and coupled by a rank-32 bilinear interaction module to explicitly capture cross-molecular interactions. The resulting pairwise representation is subsequently fed into a single positive-weighted binary classification head for co-assembly prediction. Experimental results demonstrate that MoBiTDE outperforms other methods under different evaluation settings. Notably, its predictive performance further improves as the dataset expands, highlighting the potential of pre-trained molecular representations to benefit from increasing experimental data. In summary, MoBiTDE provides an effective framework for learning drug–excipient compatibility and offers a promising computational approach to facilitate the discovery of self-assembling nanoparticle formulations. It can improve drug discovery efficiency by reducing the number of trials, focusing only wet-lab testing on promising combinations.

items.title: Modeling the Human Platform
items.abstract: Industry 4.0 research still treats sustainability, inclusivity, and workforce capability as separate concerns. This chapter proposes the Human Platform, a higher order sociotechnical capability through which technological enablement, inclusivity practices, and sustainability orientation jointly shape human adaptability and organizational performance. Drawing on Sociotechnical Systems Theory, Human Capital Theory, Dynamic Capabilities Theory, the Capability Approach, and Stakeholder Theory, the chapter develops the Human Platform Model and eight theoretical propositions linking these constructs to sustainable organizational outcomes. A proposed explanatory sequential mixed methods design is offered for future empirical validation, illustrated through documented industry cases. The chapter closes with implications for theory, management practice, and workforce policy in digitally transforming organizations.

items.title: Modelling real active learning in the realm of artificial intelligence
items.abstract: In the age of artificial intelligence (AI), learning practices surge the environment. We are at a stage of critically processing how active learning practices are still relevant in the age of AI. This chapter will critically portray the field-based impact of AI in learning engagements by rationalising students’ active learning practices within the context of AI by discussing the right way of introducing AI in education, and how significant teachers’ roles are in the use of AI. Further to these arguments, an Australian case study will be briefly discussed to show how to effectuate learning experiences and maintain student agency in that learning process. This chapter should be seen as a thought-provoking piece on how to re-examine the active learning experience from a not-so-distant past called today and into the future in the age of dynamic AI.

items.title: Multidimensional Tracing of Error Sources and Structured Corrective Strategies for Leukocyte Count and Differential on Automated Hematology Analyzers
items.abstract: Leukocyte count and differential are core indicators for clinical infection assessment, hematological disease diagnosis, and therapeutic monitoring. Currently, clinical testing heavily relies on automated hematology analyzers. Influenced by factors such as specimen characteristics, limited analyzer recognition capability, and improper manual operations, automated testing often produces unreliable results, interfering with clinical decision-making and threatening patient safety. Existing studies remain fragmented, lacking a multidimensional error-tracing framework and practical corrective strategies covering the entire testing workflow. A narrative review was conducted to summarize the causes, identification methods, and corrective strategies for unreliable leukocyte results. Relevant literature up to August 2026 was searched in PubMed/MEDLINE and CNKI. We categorized multidimensional error sources into specimen-related interferents, leukocyte morphological and developmental abnormalities, and preanalytical or systematic factors, and established a practical diagnostic workflow spanning from anomaly recognition to result reporting. By incorporating both legacy and current analytical systems, we compared the characteristic scattergram patterns of various interferents across analyzers with different detection principles, broadening the applicability to diverse clinical laboratories. To better ensure the reliability of corrective strategies and provide diverse alternative options, we not only summarized widely accepted routine practices but also included case-based experimental methods. The proposed multidimensional error-tracing system and practical diagnostic workflow significantly improve analytical accuracy and reduce clinical risks. However, current hematology analyzers cannot automatically identify or correct complex interferences. Future systems must integrate multi-platform advantages, optimize complex cell recognition capabilities, and enrich multidimensional scattergram information to overcome existing analytical limitations. Furthermore, integrating artificial intelligence technology holds immense potential to drive automated hematology analysis toward a more intelligent and precise direction.

The chapter explores the possibility of smart city infrastructure, along with IoT-enabled multimodal systems, to radically enhance traffic control and city surveillance using the assistance of drone-based capabilities.
