Multimodal data fusion architectures, scalable communication architecture, and intelligent decision-support systems are introduced in the chapter. The UAV-enabled systems have the potential to transform the field, which has been demonstrated by the most crucial applications, including emergency response, road safety assessment, and infrastructure monitoring. items.title: Multimodal Deep Learning, Longitudinal Severity Tracking, and Explainable AI in Canine Dermatology: A Review of Emerging Paradigms and Decision-Support Systems
items.abstract: This review examines emerging applications of deep learning, multimodal data fusion, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), and longitudinal severity tracking in canine dermatology. It critically synthesizes research published between 2021 and 2026, covering convolutional neural networks, EfficientNet, YOLO-based lesion detection, MobileNetV2, Vision Transformers, and the integration of clinical metadata with dermatological images. The review discusses the limitations of visual-only classification, including duplicate-image leakage, limited dataset diversity, insufficient external validation, and uncertainty in real-world clinical performance. It also examines explainability methods such as Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) and SHAP, alongside the challenges of tracking lesion severity across repeated examinations. The paper proposes the PetZoe VetScan paradigm: a veterinarian-in-the-loop decision-support architecture combining lesion detection, multimodal clinical metadata, visual explanations, uncertainty estimation, and longitudinal comparison. The proposed system is intended to support preliminary screening and monitoring rather than replace professional veterinary diagnosis or clinical judgment. Its longitudinal severity-tracking component is identified as experimental and requires further validation. The review highlights research priorities including independent external validation, diverse clinical datasets, patient-level data splitting, standardized severity assessment, transparent uncertainty communication, and prospective clinical evaluation. Keywords: Canine dermatology; deep learning; explainable artificial intelligence; Grad-CAM; longitudinal lesion tracking; multimodal clinical decision support; veterinary artificial intelligence; veterinarian-in-the-loop.

items.abstract: The development of multimodal artificial intelligence has accelerated to such a degree that the integration of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and computer vision has become possible such that systems are able to interpret, reason over, and create cross-modal content in cooperation. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can be seen as an important step in this development and, ironically, the CLIP and GPT-4V models are called Vision-Language Models because they align textual and visual representations in common embedding spaces and multimodal transformer architectures. These models help in zero-shot learning, cross-modal retrieval, visual question answering, caption generation, and multimodal reasoning, thus reducing AI capabilities from perception to contextual understanding. In the chapter, the theoretic, architectural design, and training paradigm of NLP-vision integration are explored. It also examines practical implementation in areas of healthcare diagnostics, intelligent surveillance systems, autonomous systems, e-commerce, accessibility technologies, and multimedia content analysis. Contrasting and generative multimodal methods are proven to be more beneficial in terms of accuracy, robustness, and contextual reasoning than unimodal baselines as experimentally evaluated. Moreover, the chapter includes computational, ethical, and scalability issues of implementing the use of large-scale VLMs. This publication makes a contribution to the future of AI-based multimedia and multimodal intelligence systems by offering a comprehensive framework on how researchers and practitioners should further develop algorithmic innovation in applied deployment strategies.

items.title: Multistep and Multivariate Time Series Explainability with GradientSHAP: A Wind Power Case Study
items.abstract: As the effects of climate change become increasingly apparent, the demand for renewable energy sources such as wind power continues to grow. However, renewables' variable and intermittent nature presents significant challenges in their integration into energy grids. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a powerful tool to address these issues. Still, its adoption in the energy sector has been hindered by the opacity of many AI models, which often function as black boxes. This paper introduces a carefully adapted GradientSHAP approach to provide interpretability for multivariate, multistep wind power forecasting -- a largely underexplored area. This capability is critical for day-ahead grid management and, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to apply GradientSHAP in the context of wind power forecasting. To address the inherent dimensionality, we developed novel visualizations that deliver both local and global explanations, uncovering intricate relationships between environmental factors, site-specific conditions, and temporal dynamics. While GradientSHAP is not an out-of-the-box solution, our findings demonstrate that, with thoughtful handling of SHAP values and domain expertise, it can offer valuable insights into model behaviour, supporting more informed and trustworthy decision-making. Nevertheless, its complexity poses challenges for practical implementation. Future research should focus on streamlining these interpretability methods to make them more actionable for routine deployment in critical energy applications.

items.title: Museum-Grounded Generative-AI Guide Affordances and Heritage Stewardship Intention: Evidence from Jinghui
items.abstract: Museum-grounded generative-AI guides can extend heritage interpretation from information delivery to a participatory encounter that connects what visitors understand, experience, and intend to protect. Existing research, however, rarely distinguishes whether system affordances are associated with desirable outcomes, predictively important, or necessary for those outcomes to reach high levels. Drawing on the stimulus–organism–response framework, this study develops an integrated model of how dialogic, epistemic, social, cultural, adaptive, and participatory affordances relate to perceived heritage-value enhancement, flow, stewardship self-efficacy, and pro-heritage stewardship intention. Post-interaction evidence from adults reporting prior Jinghui use was examined through partial least squares structural equation modeling, artificial neural networks, a matched Basis-KAN predictive benchmark, and necessary-condition analysis. The findings identify outcome-specific profiles: responsive dialog is prominent for perceived value enhancement; visitor agency has the highest mean ANN importance for flow; epistemic transparency and cultural authenticity are closely ranked for self-efficacy; and perceived value enhancement and flow retain necessity evidence for stewardship intention. The direct value-enhancement–self-efficacy path is unsupported. Close coefficient differences do not establish superior design features, and ANN ranks vary across fitted runs. Comparison of nonlinear importance with held-out prediction further shows that a flexible representation does not automatically yield stronger predictive performance. By linking accountable system design to visitors’ meaning-making and stewardship motivation, this study provides an evidence-informed foundation for designing museum generative AI as public interpretive infrastructure that connects cultural accountability with informed participation in heritage stewardship.

items.title: Nanobiomechanics in Oncology: Atomic Force Microscopy for Cancer Mechanophenotyping Using Cellular Young's Modulus
items.abstract: This review examines the current literature on the application of atomic force microscopy (AFM) to cancer mechanophenotyping, with particular emphasis on cellular Young's modulus and its potential diagnostic significance. A structured electronic search of PubMed, Scopus and Google Scholar was conducted to identify studies published between 1999 and 2025 reporting AFM‐based measurements of cellular Young's modulus in cancer‐related models. Across multiple malignancies, reduced cellular stiffness is frequently observed in malignant compared with non‐malignant cells and is associated with cytoskeletal remodelling, increased deformability and altered cell–matrix interactions. However, the relationship between Young's modulus and malignancy is not universally monotonic. Nanomechanical properties may vary across different pathological states and malignant phenotypes rather than following a simple monotonic trajectory, while invasive and metastatic cells can dynamically remodel their cytoskeleton and modify their stiffness in response to environmental and mechanical constraints. Young's modulus should therefore not be regarded as an isolated universal cancer biomarker, but rather as one component of a dynamic mechanophenotype influenced by disease stage, cellular region, microenvironment and measurement methodology. Recent advances in automated force acquisition, optical cell recognition, artificial intelligence and high‐throughput AFM are beginning to address traditional limitations in measurement efficiency and operator dependence. The future diagnostic value of AFM may therefore lie in integrating Young's modulus with complementary parameters, including spatial mechanical heterogeneity, viscoelasticity, adhesion, deformation‐energy characteristics and nanotopography, to define multidimensional cancer mechanophenotypes. Standardised acquisition and analysis protocols, together with validation in patient‐derived specimens, will be essential for translating AFM nanomechanics from an experimental measurement into a clinically informative biomechanical biomarker.

items.title: Navigating Emotions:
items.abstract: The number of people experiencing mental health issues is increasing around the globe and the demand for effective technology-based solutions to tackle mental health challenges continues to increase. This research aims to conduct a systematic review of Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques that have been used for the identification of emotions from conversations in the context of mobile applications for mental health support. The study has followed PRISMA guidelines for the examination of literature from the years 2017 to 2025 and categorisation of machine-learning, deep learning and transformer-based models including BERT, RoBERTa and Large Language Models (LLMs) for emotion recognition in mental health applications. The findings of the study show that transformer-based models provide the highest levels of accuracy in detecting depression, suicidal ideations and emotional distress, with an accuracy rate exceeding 90%, when applied to user generated inputs through NLP methods. Nonetheless, there are obstacles to the advancement of AI technologies for use within mental health support, including the high levels of computational power needed for mobile applications, insufficient explanations for the outputs of AI systems, and the lack of high-quality multilingual mental health data.

items.title: NEOPIC: A Neural Operator Framework for Particle-based Kinetic Plasma Simulations
items.abstract: We introduce NEOPIC, a framework for learning the field operator in particle-based methods applied to kinetic plasma simulations. Its key novelty is a neural operator that acts directly on the empirical measure of the particles, rather than on a grid, and is evaluated at the particle positions. No mesh or tree is needed and, unlike grid-based neural operators, no deposition onto a mesh takes place, so the particle noise that dominates the inputs of particle simulations is not aliased. Since it replaces only the field solve, it serves as a plug-and-play field solver for particle-based methods: it can be trained on data from particle-in-cell, particle-in-Fourier or tree codes, and combined with any time integrator, including implicit schemes. We prove that the discrete evaluation coincides with the continuous operator at any number of particles (representation equivalence) and derive an error analysis that separates sampling, learning and time-stepping errors: up to the learning error, NEOPIC has the error structure of standard Monte Carlo particle methods. We show that the particle noise in the training data acts as an implicit regularizer, which gives guidance on the number of training particles in relation to the particle numbers used at inference. A complexity analysis shows that NEOPIC is an $O(N_p)$ method whose constants are set by the architecture alone, independently of any mesh or tree. Numerical experiments on electrostatic benchmarks in two and three dimensions, including Landau damping, two-stream and bump-on-tail instabilities, a cyclotron mini-app and a Penning trap, confirm the theoretical findings. A single model trained on several mini-apps generated by different reference methods captures all of them and remains stable up to twice the training time window, which points towards foundation models for fields in particle-based methods.

items.title: Network modeling of science teachers’ perceptions of artificial intelligence integration in science curriculum development
items.abstract: Abstract This study employs psychological network modeling to examine the interrelationships among science teachers’ perceptions of benefits, challenges, and attitudes toward integrating artificial intelligence (AI) tools in science curriculum development. A total of 691 Saudi science teachers completed a validated questionnaire. Network estimation using regularization and centrality analyses identified key themes in science teachers’ perceptions of benefits, challenges, and attitudes toward integrating artificial intelligence (AI) tools into curriculum development and instructional practices. The estimated network revealed a dense structure. Centrality analyses indicated that curriculum content generation and innovative pedagogical tools were most central, while data processing challenges and algorithmic bias emerged as prominent structural barriers. Centrality metrics identify AI-facilitated curriculum design and innovative pedagogical tools as primary benefits, while challenges such as data processing limitations and algorithmic biases emerge as significant barriers. Teacher attitudes demonstrate ambivalence, characterized by resistance to automating administrative functions alongside guarded optimism for interactive and adaptive learning applications. These insights underscore the imperative to address technical constraints, ethical considerations, and the evolving professional identities of educators to ensure effective AI integration. The study contributes a nuanced, systemic understanding that informs the development of tailored AI tools and support frameworks, ultimately advancing transformative innovation in science education.

items.title: Neuralsymbolic AI for Multimodal Reasoning Combining Logic and Deep Learning
items.abstract: The conventional Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been observed to have challenges regarding interpretability and generalization when deployed in complex reasoning tasks. This setback diminishes its effectiveness in critical domains where such characteristics are required. Therefore, there has been a shift towards Neurosymbolic Artificial Intelligence (NeSyAI) to offer syntheses of neural network systems and symbolic reasoning inference. Basically, NeSyAI amalgamates symbolic thinking and deep learning through the leveraging of their synergy. As such, NeSyAI-based synthesis has been noted to be a promising paradigm that has seen an improvement in robustness, interpretability, and trustworthiness. In addition, it has capabilities of learning through comparatively small datasets. In a nutshell, the objective of neuro-symbolic reasoning is the combination of the ability to perceive and the ability to engage in logical inference. It also amalgamates deep learning with commonsense knowledge, which is a crucial requirement for intuitive visual analogy and semantically rich scene description. In this chapter, we provide some critical insights into NeSyAI, identify taxonomies, frameworks, domain-specific applications, and critical analyses of various emerging frontiers in this domain. In addition, we identify some critical research gaps in this field, which future research works can leverage on.

items.title: NeuroCare Nexus-Intelligent Remote Patient Monitoring for Home Healthcare: A Review of AI-Driven Physiological Monitoring, Anomaly Detection, Clinical Decision Support, and Connected Care
items.abstract: Remote patient monitoring (RPM) is increasingly used to extend clinical oversight into the home, particularly for people living with chronic disease. Connectivity alone does not make monitoring clinically useful: readings must be trustworthy, interpreted against the individual patient, routed to the right person, and acted upon. This focused narrative review examines intelligent RPM for home healthcare across connected themes: care-delivery evidence, physiological and activity sensing, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML), physiological anomaly detection, alerting and alarm fatigue, clinical decisionsupport, medication adherence, patient–caregiver–clinician collaboration, and security, interoperability, and reliability. Literature was identified through ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, PubMed, JMIR, and Crossref-indexed IEEE and other publisher records, with emphasis on work published from 2020 to 2026. The evidence indicates that structured RPM can benefit selected opulations, but effects vary across conditions and outcomes. Algorithm studies often report strong retrospective performance, whereas evaluated RPM interventions still rely mostly on heuristic thresholds, and few validated algorithms have been tested in clinical trials. Baseline-relative detection on wearable data has shown promise in large cohort studies, while signal artefact, false alerts, limited external validation, and weak integration of adherence and caregiver roles remain unresolved. The review identifies the comparison between generic fixed thresholds and personalized temporal models, evaluated under realistic data-quality and alert-burden conditions, as a central open question. Future home-health platforms should combine quality-aware sensing, transparent safety rules, individualized trend analysis, tiered role-aware alerting, and clinician oversight.

items.title: Next-generation cotton improvement through integrated biosynthetic pathways, multi-omics, artificial intelligence and advanced breeding technologies
items.abstract: Cotton ( Gossypium spp.) is a globally important fibre and oilseed crop whose productivity and quality are increasingly constrained by climate change, biotic stresses and the complex genetic architecture of key agronomic traits. Recent advances in genomics, high-throughput phenotyping and systems biology have transformed our understanding of cotton evolution, fibre development, stress adaptation and defence mechanisms. This review synthesizes current progress in cotton improvement through integrative approaches encompassing pan-genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics and phenomics, with particular emphasis on fibre quality regulation, secondary metabolite-mediated insect resistance and abiotic stress tolerance. We highlight how polyploidy, structural variation, homoeolog expression bias and regulatory network rewiring underpin phenotypic diversity and environmental adaptability in cotton. Furthermore, we discuss the emerging roles of artificial intelligence and machine-learning models in genomic prediction, trait mapping and decision support for precision breeding. The review also examines translational innovations, including CRISPR-based genome editing, nano-enabled delivery systems and nano-formulated inputs for sustainable pest and nutrient management. By integrating multi-omics data with AI-driven analytics, we propose a next-generation framework for accelerating cotton breeding pipelines under changing agro-ecological conditions. Despite rapid progress in Genomics, Bioinformatics, and Plant Breeding, existing reviews lack a systems-level perspective that links data generation, predictive modeling, and targeted intervention. This review addresses this gap by conceptualizing these advances as components of an integrated, data-driven breeding pipeline. This review uniquely integrates multi-omics and AI-driven approaches into a unified framework for cotton improvement, highlighting existing gaps and future opportunities. By integrating genome editing, nano-enabled delivery systems, and predictive analytics, these approaches enhance selection accuracy, reduce generation intervals, and enable high-throughput screening, collectively improving breeding efficiency, reduces breeding cycles and field-level resilience.

items.title: Not So Fast, Ambiverts: Extraverts Outperform in Face-to-Face Sales
items.abstract: Grant’s (2013)provocative work popularized the “ambivert advantage,” the notion that those in the middle of the introversion-extraversion continuum perform better in sales positions. We contend that ambiverts outperform in sales only when face-to-face communication is minimal, such as in Grant’s (2013) outbound call center study. We argue that extraverts will outperform in face-to-face sales because of their greater ability to decode nonverbal signals, process working memory when multitasking, and interpret subtle signals between others. In analyses with 363 pharmaceutical salespeople and with 277 health-wine sales representatives, we find evidence that the extraversion—performance relation takes an inverted-U shape among sellers who had limited face-to-face customer interactions and a significant, linear, and positive relation when face-to-face interaction with customers was high. These studies refine recent thinking and provide a novel, nuanced view of personality and job design among salespeople that can be used to develop selection batteries and to craft jobs better matching worker strengths.

items.title: Notes on the demise of metamodernism
items.abstract: This article proposes that the theoretical framework of ‘metamodernism’ as defined by Vermeulen and van den Akker (2010) is becoming less and less suited to capturing the present cultural, political, social and artistic moment. Following their own framework in establishing the shift from postmodernism to metamodernism, this article suggests a similar shift is taking place and provisionally dubs the coming cultural paradigm ‘technobarbarism.’ Its defining characteristics are: political, economic, cultural and aesthetic polarisation, sensibilities shaped by generative AI and algorithmic standardisation, cynicism brought about by the breakdown of the global rules-based order and by an epistemic crisis, return to absurdism as a coping mechanism, de-contextualisation of prior work into short-form content, the second death of the author, the abandoning of the image of the artist as the ideal worker, nihilism and disillusionment with digital platforms, as well as an ever-growing demand for authenticity.

items.title: Occupational Heat Exposure and Dehydration Prevention Practices in a Sugar Manufacturing Facility: A Qualitative Assessment in Lampung, Indonesia
items.abstract: Occupational heat exposure represents an important health and safety concern in the sugar manufacturing industry, where workers may experience prolonged exposure to heat generated by boilers, evaporation processes, and production machinery. Excessive heat exposure, particularly when combined with physical workload and inadequate fluid replacement, may increase the risk of dehydration and heat-related illness. This study aimed to assess occupational heat exposure conditions, existing workplace control measures, and dehydration prevention practices at a sugar manufacturing facility in Lampung, Indonesia. A descriptive qualitative approach was employed using workplace observations, field surveys, interviews with workers and company representatives, and a review of available occupational health and safety information. The assessment focused on production and boiler areas, perceived heat exposure, worker-reported symptoms, ventilation systems, personal protective equipment, drinking water availability, rest arrangements, and occupational health services. The findings were analyzed descriptively to identify existing preventive measures and potential gaps in workplace heat-stress management. The production and boiler areas were identified as workplaces with substantial potential for heat exposure due to continuous operation of processing equipment and heat-generating machinery. The facility employed approximately 485 workers and operated through three daily shifts. Workers reported experiencing hot working conditions, thirst, excessive sweating, fatigue, and dizziness during work activities. Existing occupational health measures included ventilation systems, cooling fans, personal protective equipment, access to drinking water, designated rest areas, workplace safety procedures, periodic medical examinations, and a company health clinic with 24-hour medical personnel. However, objective Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) measurements and a specific worker hydration monitoring program were not documented. Consequently, the magnitude of occupational heat exposure and the prevalence of dehydration could not be established. The findings identify potential occupational heat hazards and highlight the importance of strengthening heat-specific preventive practices within an existing occupational health and safety system. Although general workplace safety and healthcare facilities were available, systematic heat exposure assessment, worker hydration monitoring, targeted education, and exposure-appropriate work–rest arrangements require further attention. Integrating these measures into occupational health management may support more comprehensive heat-stress prevention in sugar manufacturing facilities. Further quantitative investigations are necessary to evaluate environmental heat exposure, hydration status, and the effectiveness of preventive interventions.

items.title: OI-AADX: an optimised image-based Android Adware detection using eXplainable AI
items.abstract: Existing Machine learning (ML)/Deep Learning (DL) based android malware detection approaches suffer from a series of issues viz. Adversarial Robustness, Higher Computational Complexity, Data Scarcity and Imbalance, Explainability and Interpretation, Higher False Positives and Meta/Polymorphic Nature of Malware. Our focus in this research is on two aspects viz. (a) addressing the Explainability and Interpretation issue that typically the DL-based techniques suffer from and (b) optimisation. In this paper, we propose a CNN-based adware detection method that uses an Android permission-based dataset (MadDroid). We convert the dataset permissions into black and white images and use them to train the proposed CNN model. We use eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques to get SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values and use them to find the feature’s contribution in the prediction of our model. By following this, the number of features reduces from 440 to 144 key features. We apply statistical methods to analyse SHAP values and highlight the most significant features by training and testing our model on each reduced dataset. We systematically find out the important features using CNN and XAI, and we have maintained the sequence of permission in the image to maintain the same sequence as the original feature set.

items.title: Online Dense Reinforcement Learning with Planning-Grounding Agent for UI Navigation on Live IOS Apps
items.abstract: While frontier vision-language models demonstrate strong capabilities in user interface (UI) navigation, their high inference costs prohibit everyday use. Conversely, smaller models trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or offline reinforcement learning often memorize static trajectories, leading to brittle execution and an inability to recover from errors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel online reinforcement learning framework that trains UI navigation agents directly on live iOS applications. Our framework decouples the agent into two specialized components: a Planning agent and a UI Grounding model. We rely on an LLM-as-a-Judge to provide comprehensive reward signals, combining dense, step-level feedback to evaluate intermediate progress with a terminal reward for overall task completion. To effectively leverage this dual reward structure, we optimize the agent using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with step-level advantage estimation. Furthermore, we introduce GiGPPO, a novel neighbor-conditioned value estimation method that improves critic stability by leveraging reward signals from visually similar states across concurrent trajectories. To support this online training paradigm at scale, we introduce an efficient infrastructure that orchestrates hundreds of concurrent virtual iOS devices. Evaluations on rigorous benchmarks, including UINavBench, iOSWorld, and AndroidWorld, demonstrate that our online RL trained agents substantially outperform both SFT and terminal-only RL baselines while accelerating training convergence. Notably, our 8B RL agents achieve nearly a sevenfold improvement over the SFT baseline in out-of-distribution generalization to Android environments, while outperforming Gemini-3.5-Flash and tying with Gemini-3.1-Pro on real iOS applications.

items.title: Only Accepted Tokens Count: An Energy Accounting of Speculative Decoding Under Latency Targets
items.abstract: Large language model serving is limited by facility power. Energy per token determines how many tokens a datacenter can serve, while a latency target bounds how quickly each user receives them. During decode, every weight is read from memory for every generated token. Batching amortizes this read across users but makes no individual user faster. Speculative decoding does: a drafter proposes several future tokens, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass that reuses the same weight read. Because every drafted token must be verified whether or not it is accepted, the energy speculation saves depends on how many drafted tokens are accepted. This saving is hard to pin down. It varies across target models from different attention families and across drafting schemes, and it depends on the text being served. Every drafter we evaluate accepts fewer tokens on conversation than on code, and every trained drafter accepts fewer on Romansh, a low-resource language, than on English. We measure speculative decoding under production serving conditions (SGLang, CUDA graphs enabled) on H100 and H200 GPUs, at batch sizes up to 64 across 5 corpora. On dense models, verification, not drafting, dominates the energy cost. The saving shrinks as the batch grows, because batching has already shared the weight read that speculation would divide among the accepted tokens. At large batch sizes, block drafters push verification past the balance point between arithmetic and memory traffic into the compute-bound regime, where the saving becomes a loss, and a drafter with low acceptance raises energy per token. Meeting a tighter latency target with speculation then costs additional energy. Larger batches lower energy per token without speculation. Speculation adds to that saving only when acceptance is high, and on the model we tested it leaves little headroom for latency-preserving DVFS.

items.title: ONVERSATIONAL AI FOR MENTAL HEALTH SUPPORT
items.abstract: Mental health support remains difficult to access for many individuals because of cost, stigma, limited availability of professionals, geographical barriers, and hesitation in discussing personal concerns.Conversational Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly systems based on Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Large Language Models (LLMs), offers a potential supplementary channel through which users can communicate in natural language and receive basic emotional or informational support.However, mental health is a sensitive application area in which fluent responses alone are not sufficient: reliability, contextual understanding, empathy, privacy, safety, bias, emotional dependency, and appropriate referral to human professionals are important concerns.This paper reviews the development and application of conversational AI for mental health support and synthesizes the gaps identified in the reviewed literature.Based on these gaps, a conceptual framework is proposed that combines user-input analysis, conversational context, LLM-based response generation, safety validation, and supportive response or professional referral.The framework is evaluated conceptually using eight dimensions: response relevance, empathy, context awareness, reliability, safety, privacy, usability, and transparency.The paper emphasizes that conversational AI should function as a supportive technological tool rather than a replacement for qualified mental health professionals.

items.title: Open tools for the authentic assessment of GenAI-assisted practices
items.abstract: Learning can be viewed as a process of enculturation that involves coming to understand how to use culturally relevant tools. It follows that, if we want to make valid assessments of and for learning, we need to account for how students use those tools. Traditional assessment practices tend to privilege tools in the head over tools in the world. But simply allowing students access to external tools like generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) during assessments is not sufficient to ensure validity. Hutchins’ work suggests that open tools—those that make problem steps and solutions more visible—provide wide horizons of observation and, in turn, provide evidence that can be used to make and justify assessment claims. Learning analytics platforms are one way to open up tools and widen horizons. However, current versions break the connection between tools and the cultures they represent, pulling interactions out of their authentic context of use. This chapter proposes a potential solution: we can instrument authentic tools in ways that widen our horizon of observation and move us towards more authentic assessment of GenAI-assisted practices.

items.title: Operational Security in CRDT-Based Collaborative Editing Systems
items.abstract: Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) enable real-time collaborative editing by allowing distributed participants to modify local copies of shared documents while ensuring eventual convergence. Although this architecture provides availability and synchronization benefits, it introduces significant operational security challenges when participants cannot be fully trusted. This presentation examines security limitations in CRDT-based collaborative editing systems, focusing on Yjs, Automerge, Loro, and associated synchronization infrastructures. Particular attention is given to the persistence of deleted sensitive information, document-level authorization constraints, client identity impersonation, synchronization failures caused by rejected operations, the potential loss of offline contributions, and limitations of participant revocation. The analysis incorporates technical demonstrations and reproducible experiments involving Yjs, Hocuspocus, y-websocket, and Durable Streams. These examples illustrate how malicious participants may manipulate operation identifiers, impersonate legitimate collaborators, and compromise the integrity of shared documents. A central contribution is the examination of artificial intelligence agents as active CRDT participants. The presentation demonstrates how AI-assisted editing can amplify existing authorization weaknesses through confused-deputy scenarios, excessive agency, and exposure to untrusted document content. It further discusses the implications of the Agents Rule of Two for collaborative AI systems. Practical security recommendations include separating untrusted content from editing privileges, introducing human review before applying AI-generated modifications, restricting agent capabilities through dedicated tools, assigning distinct agent identities, and implementing cryptographically verifiable operations. Fine-grained access control at the document-section level is also considered as a direction for improving collaborative editing security. The presentation highlights the need to integrate access control, identity verification, cryptographic integrity, and human oversight into the architecture of secure CRDT-based collaborative systems.

items.title: Operationalising human–AI interaction requirements through DigComp 3.0 for translator education
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is changing the landscape of translation, expanding translators’ involvement in interaction configurations, evaluation of AI-generated outputs, and governance of risks within augmented translation environments. This study defines Human–AI Interaction in Translation (HAIT) as GenAI-mediated component of the human-centred augmented translation process, where GenAI is integrated into translation technologies and conversational large language models. Translation education lacks a developmental structure that connects these emerging requirements and their related digital competences to curriculum design. This study proposes a workflow-derived operationalisation of HAIT for translator education. A conceptual functional analysis of augmented translation workflows produced eight HAIT requirements, which were mapped to the 21 competences of the European Digital Competence Framework (DigComp 3.0) by assessing 168 potential relationships for functional correspondence, scope fidelity, and traceable justification. The analysis accepted 37 relationships among 16 competences and identified translation-specific residues that require curricular supplementation. The operationalised requirements were organised into a proposed four-level progression informed by DigComp proficiency levels. An exploratory mixed-methods pilot with 42 second-year translation students examined perceived relevance after contextualised exposure in a course-embedded intervention. Students broadly perceived DigComp as relevant to translation education and practice, particularly focusing on competences related to familiar topics such as privacy protection, device security, copyright, information retrieval, communication and collaboration, with limited attention to information evaluation and programming competences. Their responses were less explicit about AI-generated output evaluation, prompting and in-context steering, grounding configuration, and risk-responsive actions, highlighting the value of a spiral curriculum for competence development and Quality Education (SDG4).

items.title: Optimized CNN Model for Real-World Plant Disease Detection
items.abstract: Agriculture is indispensable for the security of the global food supply; however, diseases that are often unnoticed in their initial stages cause a considerable decline in crop yield. Manual disease detection via traditional means is slow, requires a lot of manpower, and can result in mistakes; thus, it is not appropriate for extensive or instantaneous diagnoses. This study proposes a refined Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model tailored for reliable and automatic detection of plant diseases using images of leaves taken in the field under real-world agricultural conditions. A deep CNN that has been trained on a vast plant disease dataset shows impressive multi-class classification accuracy and at the same time, has low computational demands. Through a mobile or web interface, users can receive feedback that is nearly real-time; thus, it is affordable for farmers who use devices with low resources. The integration of artificial intelligence into the agricultural workflow has made the proposed methodology a scalable, cost-effective, and eco-friendly solution for the prompt detection of diseases and better crop management in the future.

items.title: Optogenetics in neurobiology and neurodegenerative disorders: from neural circuit mechanisms to precision neuromodulation
items.abstract: Neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis and stroke, are characterized by progressive neuronal dysfunction, synaptic impairment and neural circuit degeneration, leading to severe cognitive and motor deficits. Although considerable progress has been made in understanding their molecular pathology, the circuit level mechanisms driving disease onset and progression remain incompletely understood. Optogenetics, which combines microbial opsins, genetic engineering and optical stimulation, enables reversible, cell-specific control of neuronal activity with millisecond precision and has transformed neuroscience from observational analysis to causal investigation of neural circuits. This review summarizes recent advances in the molecular basis of optogenetics, microbial opsins, gene delivery strategies and optical stimulation technologies, together with their applications in basic neurobiology and neurodegenerative disease research. We discuss how optogenetics has advanced understanding of neural circuit organization, synaptic plasticity, memory, neurodevelopment, sleep regulation, protein aggregation, synaptic dysfunction, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial impairment, oxidative stress and regulated cell death. Although these studies have generated important mechanistic insights and demonstrated functional improvements in experimental models, translation into human therapies remains investigational due to challenges associated with gene delivery, long-term opsin expression, immune compatibility and optical accessibility. Emerging therapeutic strategies, including closed-loop neuromodulation, wireless photostimulation, artificial intelligence-assisted neural decoding, nanotechnology enabled light delivery and brain computer interfaces, are critically evaluated with emphasis on their current evidence status, translational challenges and limitations for clinical implementation. Collectively, optogenetics provides an unprecedented platform for deciphering disease mechanisms and evaluating circuit-based neuromodulation strategies, while continued technological and biological validation will determine its future role in precision therapies for neurodegenerative disorders.

items.title: Organizations in Interaction With Stakeholders and the Environment
items.abstract: Organizations operate in complex environments shaped by stakeholders, institutions, regulations, technologies and societal expectations. Their ability to survive, adapt and create value depends not only on internal capabilities but also on their responses to external pressures and on maintaining legitimacy. Relationships among organizations, stakeholders and organizational environments shape organizational priorities, resource access and opportunities for action. Stakeholder theory, legitimacy and institutional perspectives offer important lenses for understanding how organizations gain support, secure resources and maintain their licence to operate. Governments, customers, employees, investors, communities and advocacy groups all influence organizational choices, often in different and competing ways. Broader environmental forces, including digitalization, artificial intelligence, sustainability challenges, globalization and regulatory change, create both opportunities and constraints. These developments generate new expectations, strategic dilemmas and pressures to adapt. Organizations are embedded within social, economic, political, technological and ecological systems, making context central to organizational analysis and practice.

items.title: Originality as texture
items.abstract: Conventional notions of originality position university students as the sole authors of the work they submit for assessment. This means that originality is seen as a kind of academic alchemy, whereby students draw from other sources to complete their work but must somehow transform it into something that is wholly of themselves. In this chapter, we propose an alternative framing of originality—as a texture of contributions—to acknowledge the interwoven nature of how students produce work with artificial intelligence (AI). The key distinction is that students’ interactions with AI (or others) are understood as textural rather than absolute. In contrast to approaches which attempt to fully disentangle human and AI, this perspective reorients assessment design to consider two different foci for assurance: work and working . Most current assessment focuses on fixed outputs (work), whether interim or final, to assure achievement. However, this approach cannot assure students’ ways of working, which we argue requires assessors to be participants in the dynamic activity involved in generating work. By being participants in working, assessors can more fully understand the nature of students’ contributions to the work they submit for assessment, and so can make further assurances about the originality of that work.

items.title: Participant-Specific Adaptive Label Smoothing Using Subjective Workload Responses for Cognitive Workload Classification from EEG
items.abstract: Background: Cognitive workload classification from electroencephalography is affected by interindividual variability in EEG signals and subjective workload responses. We propose participant-specific adaptive label smoothing, in which the change in perceived workload between resting and task conditions controls the target confidence, while the experimental class remains unchanged. Methods: The method was evaluated on the STEW dataset and compared with five alternative supervision strategies. Two classification models were used: a feature-based convolutional neural network and a multi-scale Swin Transformer network (MST-Net) operating on time-frequency representations. Global and participant-specific stratified normalization were evaluated using participant-disjoint cross-validation. The participant-specific approach used normalization statistics estimated from each unseen participant’s own unlabeled EEG data. Results: Under stratified normalization, adaptive label smoothing produced the highest macro F1 for both models, with values of 0.768 and 0.796, and ROC AUC values of 0.844 and 0.878, respectively. It also maintained high recall for both classes. Conclusions: The findings suggest that participant-specific subjective workload responses can be used to modulate target confidence, with the most consistent benefit observed under participant-specific normalization. As the strategies differ in target definitions and no hard rest/task or fixed label-smoothing control was evaluated, the differences are descriptive.

items.title: PathCowork: Learning from real-world pathology practice to build AI copilots
items.abstract: Medical AI learns from the answers doctors record, but rarely from how they interpret the evidence to reach them. Here we introduce PathCowork, a framework that turns pathologists' narrated examinations into supervision for visual grounding and procedures that guide diagnostic AI agents. Synchronized gaze, narration and navigation link visual findings to the process of interpreting them. Across 48 sessions from 16 pathologists, the platform captured 1,028 minutes of slide review. Using these data, we trained PathCowork-1T for server deployment and PathCowork-27B for local deployment, with improved visual grounding. Across five organ-specific evaluations, agents combining this grounding with recorded diagnostic procedures achieved primary task scores averaging 17.9 and 24.1 percentage points higher than Claude Code and Codex, respectively, with shorter processing times and lower inference costs. Compared to the state-of-the-art multiple-instance learning AIs, the PathCowork agent-proposed regions achieved higher prostate-grading scores with limited slide labels. PathCowork can also help construct pathology AI benchmarks where questions derived from the recordings identified difficulties in recognizing viewing context and rejecting inapplicable premises. In summary, PathCowork proposes a new paradigm to scale up the data collection and train pathology AI through transparent reasoning from diagnostic sessions, opening a path towards systems that learn directly from routine clinical practice.

items.title: PCM: A Proof-Carrying Message Protocol for Verifiable Multi-Agent Communication
items.abstract: When one AI agent tells another that "the tests passed" or "a person approved this refund", the receiver has only the sender's word. A2A and MCP authenticate the channel, but the sender is the party in doubt, so a prompt-injected agent can launder fabricated facts and authority through a multi-agent system. We present Proof-Carrying Messages (PCM), a protocol in which each claim carries evidence: records from an append-only Merkle log that the agent cannot write, with inclusion proofs, signed by an attesting signer the agent cannot control. Receivers check messages offline and give each claim a three-valued result: proven, unproven or failed. A claim that rests only on the agent's own report is never proven. Authority travels as grant chains rooted in a recorded human approval, and the chains can only narrow. We specify four claim types, a typed caveat algebra, replay rules that survive restarts, and strict readings that make independent verifiers agree, and we prove the resulting security properties. On a pre-specified benchmark of 926 messages from real runs, 712 of them lies in 16 classes, PCM accepts 10 lies, all of them stale evidence (1.4%, 95% CI 0.8-2.6%). Plain A2A accepts all 712, and models of six deployed protocols (A2A with signed Agent Cards, uAgents, RFC 9421, SCITT, AP2, Verifiable Intent) accept 504-712. Two independent verifiers agree on all 926 verdicts, and verification takes about 1 ms.

items.title: Pediatrician attitudes, acceptance, and concerns regarding artificial intelligence in pediatric care: a web-based survey in Türkiye
items.abstract: In Türkiye, pediatricians’ perspectives on artificial intelligence (AI), including their knowledge, trust, and concerns, remain underexplored. This study aims to evaluate pediatricians’ knowledge, perceptions, and acceptance of AI in pediatric care. A cross-sectional, open, web-based convenience survey was conducted among pediatricians in Türkiye, including residents and specialists. The survey assessed their knowledge of AI, perceptions of its benefits and risks, and acceptance of AI as a clinical decision support tool. A total of 403 pediatricians accessed the survey; 18 declined to participate, 1 was excluded for a completion time under two minutes, and 16 were excluded for an inconsistent control-item. After excluding responses, 368 were included in the analysis. Participants had a median age of 35 years and a median of 9 years of pediatric care experience. Only 9.5% of participants reported awareness of AI in pediatrics, and 85.9% rated their self-perceived AI knowledge as average or below. Despite this, 74.2% agreed that AI will improve pediatrics, and 88.3% stated it could enhance care quality. Concerns included legal liability (78.5%), data security (54.6%), and the black-box nature of AI (59.2%). Across all 37 ordinal items, a single age correlation survived: younger respondents were more likely to expect AI to increase diagnostic confidence (r s = -0.171, 95% CI -0.269 to -0.070, small effect size; P = 0.001; P adj = 0.038). While 90.8% supported AI as a clinical decision support tool, only 17.4% believed AI could replace human physicians in non-invasive roles. Only 19.3% expected their institution to allocate financial or personnel resources for AI integration. Survey respondents generally view AI as a promising tool to improve pediatric care but express significant concerns about its reliability, ethical implications, and legal responsibilities.

items.abstract: The development of artificial intelligence in education opens up opportunities to support learning while also raising ethical issues related to academic integrity and students’ digital responsibility. This article aims to analyze the role of character education as a foundation for guiding the use of artificial intelligence in relation to these two aspects. The study employs a literature review using a descriptive-qualitative approach. The findings indicate that the values of ṣidq and amanah provide a conceptual foundation for transparency in AI use, recognition of intellectual contributions, adherence to assignment guidelines, and accountability for learning processes and outcomes. Meanwhile, the values of tabayyun, respect for others, and a focus on the common good underpin digital responsibility in the form of information verification, privacy protection, respect for intellectual property, and consideration of the social impacts of AI use. Strengthening these two aspects requires educators to lead by example, clear institutional guidelines, family support, and reflective learning grounded in ethical dilemmas. This article concludes that the integration of character education and AI literacy should be directed toward developing students who are proficient in using technology while also being able to make decisions honestly and responsibly. The resulting conceptual framework still requires empirical testing according to educational levels and contexts.

items.title: Penguatan Kompetensi Guru dalam Mengembangkan Media Pembelajaran Interaktif Menggunakan Canva AI
items.abstract: Teachers' competence in designing technology-based interactive learning media is one of the key factors for successful 21st-century learning. However, initial mapping at SMP Plus Aisyah Samawa revealed that approximately 70% of teachers still relied on conventional learning media, and more than 80% were unfamiliar with the Artificial Intelligence (AI) features of the Canva design platform, such as Magic Design, AI Presentation, and Text to Image. This community service program aimed to strengthen teachers' technical and pedagogical competence in developing interactive learning media using Canva AI, integrated with lesson plans (RPP) or teaching modules. The program was implemented in three stages: preparation, implementation (socialization, hands-on training with a 30% theory–70% practice composition, and classroom technology application), and evaluation, supported by three months of intensive post-training mentoring. Program success indicators were measured through pretest–posttest score improvements, the percentage of teachers producing interactive learning media products, and the integration of such media into lesson plans or teaching modules. The results showed an improvement in teachers' competence in utilizing Canva's AI features and an increase in student engagement during the learning process. This program is expected to serve as a replicable model for strengthening teachers' digital literacy in other pesantren-based schools in Sumbawa Regency, while contributing to the achievement of SDG 4 (Quality Education) and SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure).

items.title: Perancangan Alat Bantu Ergonomis untuk Menunjang Perilaku Disiplin Anak Melalui Pendekatan Bio-mimikri
items.abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to design and develop furniture as a medium or assistive tool to foster children’s disciplined behavior in returning their belongings to designated places at home. Methodology: The study employed an ergonomic product design approach integrated with a biomimicry design method. Findings: The study produced a piece of furniture whose form and colors resemble the fruit of the Patuk Manuk plant (Thunbergia alata). Observations indicated that the product created an enjoyable experience for children when placing their belongings neatly and systematically. The System Usability Scale (SUS) yielded a score of 80, indicating good usability, while the Godspeed questionnaire demonstrated high reliability, with a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.93. Conclusion: The study developed an ergonomic assistive product that supports the development of disciplined behavior in children. The product demonstrated good usability, was well accepted by both children and parents, and provided an enjoyable experience for users interacting with it. Originality: The design integrates ergonomic product design and biomimicry, a combination that remains relatively uncommon in innovative product development. Integrating these approaches is expected to provide complementary benefits in developing learning aids that support the formation of disciplined habits among children in the home environment.

items.title: Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence, Naturalistic Decision-Making and Cognitive Flexibility: A Systematic Literature Review and an Integrated Mediation Model
items.abstract: This study systematically reviews the literature on the relationships between individuals' perceptions of artificial intelligence, naturalistic decision-making and cognitive flexibility, and synthesizes the evidence into an integrated model in which cognitive flexibility mediates the effect of artificial intelligence perceptions on naturalistic decision-making. Following the PRISMA 2020 statement, three Boolean searches corresponding to the pairwise relationships were run in OpenAlex on 20 October 2026 and complemented by backward and forward citation tracking. Of 1,161 records identified, 1,140 were screened, 99 were assessed in full and 70 met the eligibility criteria; together with 32 studies reached through citation tracking, 102 studies were coded and synthesized thematically. The synthesis shows that the three constructs have been studied in largely separate streams: research on artificial intelligence and decision-making concentrates on advice-taking, reliance and decision-making styles; research on artificial intelligence and cognitive flexibility is very recent, concentrated in educational and health settings and consistent in sign; and research on cognitive flexibility and decision-making draws on laboratory, neurophysiological and survey evidence. Cognitive flexibility is a replicated mediator in adjacent domains, but no study has tested the full chain from artificial intelligence perceptions through cognitive flexibility to naturalistic decision-making. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, Cognitive Load Theory, Cognitive Flexibility Theory and the recognition-primed decision model, the study formulates four testable propositions, presents an integrated model, identifies measurement options and outlines a research agenda.

items.title: PhysCount: Do MLLMs Count Visual Appearances or Physical Entities?
items.abstract: Images reveal appearances, but counting often asks about physical objects. A single entity may be visible directly, in several reflections, or through glass, so detecting every visible occurrence does not determine how many entities are present. Existing visual counting benchmarks rarely separate these two operations. We introduce PhysCount, a benchmark for evaluating whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can distinguish what appears in an image from what physically exists in the scene. PhysCount contains 546 real-world images and 4,595 human-written questions organized into 651 target-specific groups. For each group, annotators locate the relevant appearances, label how each is observed, and identify appearances of the same entity. Four complementary question families test the enumeration of appearances, the enumeration of physical entities, image-formation-specific counting, and appearance--entity correspondence. We measure both accuracy on each family and the proportion of groups answered entirely correctly. Across 40 MLLMs, counting visible appearances is substantially easier than recovering the identities that connect them. Even the strongest model answers every question correctly in only 13.36\% of groups. Performance declines when one entity produces many appearances or when its appearances cross observation modes. Higher image resolution improves access to visual evidence but brings limited gains in complete-group accuracy, whereas answering related questions jointly produces a marked improvement. These results expose a gap between recognizing what is visible and correctly recovering the physical entities behind those observations.

items.title: Pilot Assessments of Terminal-Area Logic and Equipage-Specific Symbols While Using the Airborne Collision Avoidance System Xr During Uncrewed Operations
items.abstract: Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems (RPAS) operations are expected to increase traffic complexity in terminal-area airspace, creating new challenges for tactical separation assurance and pilot decision-making. This study evaluated subjective pilot responses to the latest version of the Airborne Collision Avoidance System for rotorcraft (ACAS Xr) during simulated RPAS operations in approach, departure, and en-route conditions. Eleven IFR-rated fixed-wing pilots completed simulated flight scenarios using ACAS Xr, including encounters involving cooperative and non-cooperative traffic and dynamic terminal-area logic. Subjective measures were collected and included workload, usability, and operational acceptability. Pilots rated ACAS Xr positively for guidance effectiveness, safe separation support, and traffic-symbol clarity for aircraft equipped and not equipped with Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast. However, terminal-area warning alerts were sometimes perceived as untimely or operationally inappropriate, particularly Level Off and Descend advisories. Results support continued development of ACAS Xr while highlighting areas requiring refinement for terminal-area operations.

items.title: Precision Medicine Using Artificial Intelligence and Genomics: A Comprehensive Review
items.abstract: Precision medicine is an emerging healthcare paradigm that tailors prevention, diagnosis, and treatment to individual patients using genetic, clinical, environmental, and lifestyle information. Advances in next-generation sequencing, bioinformatics, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) now allow clinicians to analyse genomic variants, stratify disease risk, and select therapies at a level of individual detail that population-averaged medicine cannot provide. This paper reviews AI-enabled precision medicine, synthesising landmark and recent peer-reviewed literature published between 2004 and 2026, and tracing the field from early blood-group stratification through the Human Genome Project to national precision medicine programmes and the multimodal AI of the present day. A conceptual framework is proposed that integrates electronic health records, genomic sequencing, laboratory tests, and wearable-device data in a secure platform where AI models identify biomarkers, predict risk, and recommend treatment for clinician validation; it is synthesised from literature-reported practices rather than experimentally validated. Applications in oncology, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, rare genetic disorders, pharmacogenomics, and remote monitoring are examined, followed by the main challenges, including data privacy, algorithmic bias, unrepresentative genomic datasets, cost, interpretability, and ethics, together with mitigation strategies. Emerging directions, including digital twins, federated learning, multimodal AI, and CRISPR-assisted therapies, are discussed. This review highlights the role of AI and genomics in moving healthcare from reactive to predictive and personalised, and identifies priorities for future research.

items.title: Predictive modeling and multi-objective optimization of 3D-printed PLA parts using a hybrid random vector functional link (RVFL) and henry gas solubility optimization (HGSO) framework
items.abstract: To forecast the mechanical characteristics of 3D printed Polylactic Acid (PLA) specimens, this work explores artificial intelligence models. Tensile strength (TS) and surface roughness (Ra) of printed parts were examined in relation to five process parameters: build angle (BA), infill angle (IA), layer thickness (LT), printing speed (PS), and nozzle temperature (NT). In the machine learning modelling stage models such as Random Vector Functional Link (RVFL), Random Vector Functional Link tuned by Henry Gas Solubility Optimization (RVFL-HGSO), and Artificial Neural Network (ANN) were created to forecast the printed parts’ surface roughness and tensile strength. Moreover this study shows the effectiveness of random vector functional link model tuned by the Henry Gas Solubility Optimization (RVFL-HGSO) when predicting surface roughness. The developed model achieved highest R2 = 98.95%, RMSE = 0.777, MAPE = 1.002%, and MAE = 0.514 on test dataset. It increased R2 by 4.98% when compared with RVFL and by 9.93% when compared with ANN on test dataset. RVFL-HGSO decreased MAPE by 49.93%, also MAE by 53.90%, and RMSE by 29.68% when compared with RVFL on test dataset. It also, decreased MAPE by 69.02%, also MAE by 73.95%, and RMSE by 58.49% when compared with ANN. The multi-objective optimization by particle swarm optimization (MOPSO) gives best possible solution at place of BA = 44.16, NT = 220, IA = 14.93, LT = 0.22, PS = 45.18: Minimum predicted Ra = 2.53 and maximum predicted TS = 44.15. The findings demonstrate the RVFL-HGSO model’s unique method for finding intricate correlations in the dataset, laying the groundwork for better product design and mechanical property optimization through process parameter adjustment.

items.title: Predictors of Lower Back Musculoskeletal Disability Among Emergency Department Healthcare Professionals: A Multicenter Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: Background: Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs), particularly lower back (LB) pain are highly prevalent in emergency department (ED) healthcare professionals with significant health-related impacts due to the high and unexpected workload. Objective: This study aimed to identify the predictors of LB disability among ED healthcare professionals in Jordan, including physical, psychological, and ergonomic occupational factors. Methods: A multicenter convenience sample of ED healthcare professionals was recruited from Jordanian ED departments. Data collection included demographics, ergonomics-related factors and a group of validated outcome measures: the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and the Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale (DASS-21). A stepwise multivariable linear regression model was used to identify predictors of LB disability. Results: The study included 447 participants, of whom 57% were male ( n = 255) and had a mean age of 35.1 ± 7.0 years. Predictors of the ODI ( R 2 = .31) included depression ( B = 0.456, p < .001), taking sick leave in the past 12 months (β = 6.8, p < .001), safe handling and posturing practices ( B = −5.584, p < .001), age ( B = 0.32, p < .001) and presence of musculoskeletal injury in the past 12 months ( B = 4.6, p = .022). Conclusion: This study highlights the burden of LB disability among ED healthcare professionals. LB disability was significantly associated with depression, recent Musculoskeletal injury, Musculoskeletal-related sick leave and older age, with safe handling and posture practices showing a protective effect.
